findings.title: A PowerBrowser crash leaves orcad, its terminal daemon and every skip-permissions agent running with nothing to stop them
findings.description: OrcaService has only two ways to end orcad: the quit-granted observer (line 88) and the named AsyncShutdown blocker (line 96). Neither runs when the browser crashes, is OOM-killed or gets SIGKILL. orcad has no parent-death watchdog. 62-RESEARCH item 2 confirms this, and orca-service-live depends on it ('proves orcad survived'). The terminal daemon runs detached in its own systemd user scope (daemon-cgroup-scope.ts), so killing the browser's cgroup does not end it either. The only cleanup is _reapLeftover at the next launch on the same profile. Until then, orcad keeps listening on 127.0.0.1:26768 holding the persisted device rows, and agents launched with D-12's skip-permissions keep executing tool calls (including ones steered by prompt injection) with no visible UI. D-07 says agents end when PowerBrowser quits. A crash is not a quit, so this gap is not covered by any decision.
findings.scenario: An agent is mid-task in an Orca terminal. PowerBrowser segfaults or the kernel OOM-kills it. The user does not relaunch for hours. The agent keeps running shell commands and network calls with skip-permissions, and orcad stays bound on 26768. Nothing in the tree stops either one before the next PowerBrowser start on that profile.
findings.evidence: OrcaService.sys.mjs:88 `this._quitObserverOff = PowerBrowserAPI.onQuitGranted(() => this.stop());` and :96 `PowerBrowserProcesses.addNamedReapBlocker(OrcaEnv.ORCAD_REAP_BLOCKER_NAME, reapBlocker);` are the only stop paths. :422 `proc = await PowerBrowserProcesses.spawnProcessExact({ command: this._nodePath, args, environment, workdir: this._effectiveRoot });` passes no liveness channel. Upstream orcad/main.ts and orcad-entry.ts contain no stdin-EOF or ppid watch. orcad-daemon-supervision.ts:1 says 'Detached terminal daemons must outlive orcad'. Leftovers are reaped only at the next start: OrcaService.sys.mjs:113 `await this._reapLeftover({ includeDaemon: true });`.
findings.suggested_fix: Give orcad a liveness tie to the browser. Two options: a small launcher seam that exits orcad, and has the daemon tree reaped, when its stdin pipe from PowerBrowser reaches EOF (the pattern the Theia backend's parent-death watchdog already uses); or a PB-owned watchdog process that holds the pipe and ends the recorded identities when it closes. Add a live row that SIGKILLs PowerBrowser and requires the agent identities to be gone within a bound, not merely reaped at the next launch.
findings.preconditions: PowerBrowser ends without a granted quit (crash, SIGKILL, OOM kill, power-loss-free session kill) while orcad is running.

votes.reasoning: OrcaService has two stop paths and both run only on a granted quit: onQuitGranted (OrcaService.sys.mjs:88) and the AsyncShutdown appShutdownConfirmed blocker (:96, PowerBrowserAPI.sys.mjs:11052-11057). spawnProcessExact (PowerBrowserAPI.sys.mjs:10995) is a plain Subprocess.call with no IPC channel, so orcad's 'launcher disconnect' shutdown (orcad-lifecycle.ts:89-93) needs bundledLauncherChannel plus process.send and is never armed. orcad ignores SIGHUP (orcad-lifecycle.ts:85). It also ignores EPIPE/EIO from a closed output pipe (orcad-process-error-guards.ts:55-60), so losing the parent's stdout/stderr does not end it either. Idle exit does not apply: orcad-managed-idle-exit.ts:1,22 says user-started servers never idle out and live terminals block idle exit. The daemon is detached by design (orcad-daemon-supervision.ts:1). The only cleanup is _reapLeftover at the next start (:113). D-07 covers quit only, so no decision accepts the crash case. Severity stays medium: it is a gap in process lifetime, and the agents running unattended are the user's own agents with D-12 permissions; an attacker gains no new boundary crossing from it.
votes.guard_or_evidence: No guard. OrcaService.sys.mjs:88,96 are quit-only. orcad-process-error-guards.ts:55-60 ignores EPIPE. orcad-lifecycle.ts:85 ignores SIGHUP. orcad-managed-idle-exit.ts:22 says paired servers never idle out.

findings.title: Restart Orca from the failure page kills the adopted terminal daemon and the agents that survived an orcad crash
findings.description: After an unexpected orcad exit, _supervise keeps _daemonPid and reaps with includeDaemon:false, so the daemon and its agent terminals stay alive for the next orcad to adopt (the comment at line 356: 'only a quit ends agents (D-07)'). If every respawn attempt fails, the state becomes failed and the failure page offers Restart. restart() runs _startSequence, which calls _reapLeftover({ includeDaemon: true }). That reads the state file, which still names the adopted daemon, and _endDaemon SIGTERMs and then SIGKILLs the daemon and every descendant. A user who presses Restart to get Orca back loses every running agent session and terminal that the crash path had kept alive on purpose.
findings.scenario: An agent runs a long task. orcad crashes, and during the backoff another process takes port 26768, or orcad crashes again before ready five times, so the state is failed. The user frees the port and clicks Restart Orca. _reapLeftover({includeDaemon:true}) kills the daemon from pb-orca-state.json along with its 'sleep 900' / agent descendants, and the user's in-progress agent work is gone.
findings.evidence: OrcaService.sys.mjs:165 `this._restartRun = this._startSequence().catch(err => this.reportUnexpectedFailure(err));` -> :113 `await this._reapLeftover({ includeDaemon: true });` -> :369-370 `if (own && includeDaemon) { await this._endDaemon(own.daemonPid, own.daemonTicks);`. The crash path is the opposite: :590 `await this._reapLeftover({ includeDaemon: false });`.
findings.suggested_fix: Have restart() reap with includeDaemon:false when this._daemonPid still matches its recorded identity (an adopted daemon exists). Reserve the daemon reap for a cold start, where the record comes from a previous browser session.
findings.preconditions: orcad exits unexpectedly while agents run, every respawn attempt then fails, and the user presses Restart Orca.

votes.reasoning: _supervise (:574-595) leaves _daemonPid in place and reaps with includeDaemon:false (:590). _launch retries also reap with includeDaemon:false (:402). A failed _spawnAndGate never rewrites pb-orca-state.json, because writeStateFile at :508 runs only after a ready line. The state file therefore still names the adopted daemon. When the attempts run out or a port/lock code is non-recoverable (:395-396, :480-485), _fail sets the state to failed. restart() (:156-166) is allowed in that state and runs _startSequence, which calls _reapLeftover({includeDaemon:true}) (:113). That reaches _endDaemon(own.daemonPid, own.daemonTicks) (:369-370), which takes a snapshot of listProcessTree([pid]) (:335), SIGTERMs, and SIGKILLs every remaining row (:349). The ticks match, so the identity check passes. P67-06 says restart 'reaps as the launch path does', but it does not address the adopted daemon, and this contradicts the intent stated at :356-357.
votes.guard_or_evidence: No guard. Path: OrcaService.sys.mjs:165 -> :113 -> :369-370 -> :333-349. The crash path deliberately uses includeDaemon:false at :590 and :402.

findings.title: Fixed loopback port 26768 lets any local user deny Orca to PowerBrowser by binding it first
findings.description: The orcad port is a fixed, published constant, and a busy port is deliberately non-recoverable: no retry, no other port. TCP ports on 127.0.0.1 are not per-user, so another local user or any same-user process can bind 127.0.0.1:26768 before PowerBrowser starts, and Orca then never starts for that session. This is fail-closed: PowerBrowser does not adopt the squatter (T-62-09), and the client's E2EE pinned key means a stale offer sent to a squatter does not reveal the device token. Availability is still lost, and the only recovery is editing a pref by hand. The squat also works in the gap between an orcad crash and its respawn, which sends a running session to the failed state.
findings.scenario: A second local account runs `nc -l 127.0.0.1 26768`. Every PowerBrowser launch by the victim shows the port-in-use failure page, and the Orca tabs never open.
findings.evidence: powerbrowser-sidecar.js:69 `pref("powerbrowser.orca.port", 26768);`; OrcaService.sys.mjs:238 `this._port = PowerBrowserAPI.getIntPref("powerbrowser.orca.port", 26768);`; :480-486 `const code = [OrcaEnv.ORCAD_PINNED_PORT_CODE, OrcaEnv.ORCAD_LOCK_HELD_CODE].find(c => text.includes(c)); ... return { ok: false, recoverable: false, ...`
findings.suggested_fix: When the pinned port is busy at a cold start, fall back to a port PowerBrowser picks from its own range and records in the state file and the hand-off. Keep refusing adoption. At minimum, show the holder's uid (from /proc/net/tcp) in the diagnostics rows so the user can tell a squatter from a leftover.
findings.preconditions: Another local process binds 127.0.0.1:26768 before orcad, at startup or during a respawn.

votes.reasoning: powerbrowser-sidecar.js:69 pins 26768, and OrcaService reads the same default (:238). The bind failure surfaces as pinned_port_unavailable from orcad's ws-transport. _spawnAndGate classifies it as non-recoverable (:480-485), so there is one attempt and no other port. Any local account can bind an unprivileged loopback port first. The failure is fail-closed: the squatter is never adopted, and the offer is written only after a verified ready line from PB's own child. Recovery is wider than the finding says. port-in-use is in REPAIR_AFTER (orca-hosting-status.ts:43), and its failure page renders Restart, so a same-user squatter can be stopped and Restart pressed. A different user's squatter still requires the pref change. The effect is availability only.
votes.guard_or_evidence: Fail-closed by design (OrcaService.sys.mjs:483-485 comment). Only availability is lost. Restart is offered for port-in-use (orca-hosting-status.ts:43; 67-CONTEXT P67-06).

findings.title: The terminal daemon's identity is taken from whatever process holds the reported pid now, not from the daemon's own record
findings.description: The PID-reuse defence (D-111) works only if the recorded start ticks belong to the intended process. For orcad, the lock file records linuxStartTicks itself. For the daemon, OrcaService reads the start ticks of ready.daemonPid at ready time. ready.daemonPid comes from orcad's daemon pid record (orcad-health.ts: `pid: record?.pid ?? null`), and that record is reported even when the daemon state is 'degraded' or 'absent' (self-test 'no-daemon'). If the record is stale and the pid now belongs to an unrelated process of the user, PowerBrowser stores that process's ticks as the daemon's identity. At quit, _endDaemon then SIGTERMs it and SIGKILLs its whole descendant tree, and the next cold start's reap does the same from pb-orca-state.json.
findings.scenario: After a reboot the data root still holds an old daemon pid record. The daemon fails to come up, so health is degraded or absent with a stale pid, and that pid now belongs to the user's editor. PowerBrowser records the editor's ticks as daemonTicks, and on quit the editor and its children are killed.
findings.evidence: OrcaService.sys.mjs:503-504 `this._daemonPid = ready.daemonPid; this._daemonTicks = ready.daemonPid ? await PowerBrowserAPI.readProcessStartTicks(ready.daemonPid) : null;` ; :657 `await this._endDaemon(this._daemonPid, this._daemonTicks, ...)` ; :335 `listProcessTree([pid])` then :349 `_killSnapshot(rows, null)` (SIGKILL). orca/src/main/orcad/orcad-health.ts:123 `pid: record?.pid ?? null` with state possibly 'absent'/'degraded'.
findings.suggested_fix: Record a daemon identity only when health.terminalDaemon.state is 'live', and check the pid's ppid against orcad's pid (or its /proc cmdline against the daemon entry path) before storing ticks. Better, have the ready line or the daemon pid record carry the daemon's own start ticks, as orcad.lock does.
findings.preconditions: orcad reports a stale daemon pid record, and that pid has been reused by another process of the user.

votes.reasoning: The stated scenario (a stale daemon pid record after a reboot, reported while the daemon fails to come up) cannot occur. orcad-health.ts collectTerminalDaemonHealth returns pid:null whenever getDaemonEndpointFacts() is null. getDaemonEndpointFacts (daemon-provider-state.ts:53-56) is null unless an adapter is installed. installDaemonProvider runs only at daemon-provider-init.ts:170, after newSpawner.ensureRunning() succeeded at :75. ensureRunning either adopts a daemon that answers on its socket or spawns a new one, and the new daemon writes its own pid record. After a reboot, no old daemon answers, so the record is fresh. If daemon start fails, initDaemonPtyProvider throws before the install, startOrcadDaemon returns 'unavailable', and the reported pid is null. That leaves a residual race: the adopted or spawned daemon crashes in the few seconds between adoption and OrcaService's readProcessStartTicks at :504, and its pid is reused in that window. That is far narrower than the finding claims and is not the stated path.
votes.guard_or_evidence: orca/src/main/daemon/daemon-provider-init.ts:75 (ensureRunning) and :170 (installDaemonProvider only after success). daemon-provider-state.ts:53-56 (no adapter means no facts). orcad-health.ts collectTerminalDaemonHealth returns pid:null when facts are null.

findings.title: A quit that lands just after orcad's ready line can leave the pairing credential file behind after exit
findings.description: _stopTree removes the three bridge files first (lines 630-636) and then ends orcad. _spawnAndGate does not check _shuttingDown again after outcome.ready resolves. It goes on to await readProcessStartTicks, writeStateFile and writePrivateFile(orcad-data-root), then _writeHandOff writes web-pairing and orca-panes-dir, and finally sets _state = 'ready'. If stop() starts during those awaits, the removal can run before the writes, so the web-pairing file (a reusable credential) and the other hand-off files remain in the bridge folder after the browser exits. The state can also report 'ready' after 'stopped'. The file is 0600 in a 0700 folder, so exposure is limited to the same user. The next session then consumes it as a stale offer (see the stale hand-off finding).
findings.scenario: The user quits within a second of launch while orcad is printing its ready line. _stopTree deletes web-pairing, then _writeHandOff recreates it. PowerBrowser exits with <alias>-bridge/web-pairing still on disk.
findings.evidence: OrcaService.sys.mjs:490-531 has no `_shuttingDown` check between `const ready = outcome.ready;` and `await this._writeHandOff(offer); ... this._state = "ready";`, while :630-636 `for (const name of this._bridgeDir ? [OrcaEnv.ORCAD_DATA_ROOT_FILE, OrcaEnv.ORCA_WEB_PAIRING_FILE, OrcaEnv.ORCA_PANES_DIR_FILE] : []) { ... removeStateFile(...) }` runs first in _stopTree.
findings.suggested_fix: Re-check this._shuttingDown after each await between ready and _writeHandOff, and skip the writes (and endOwn) when set. Alternatively, have _stopTree remove the bridge files again after the process is gone.
findings.preconditions: stop() begins in the short window between orcad's ready line and the end of _writeHandOff.

votes.reasoning: stop() sets _shuttingDown and _stopTree first awaits removal of the three bridge files (:630-636). In parallel, _spawnAndGate continues after outcome.ready with no _shuttingDown check: readProcessStartTicks x2 (:502,:504), writeStateFile (:508), writePrivateFile(orcad-data-root) (:523), then _writeHandOff writes web-pairing and orca-panes-dir (:552,:567). Its last check is at :434, before the race. _stopTree does not remove the bridge files a second time; it removes only the state file (:658-664). It also waits up to graceMs+500 for orcad to exit (:652), so the late writes finish before the process ends. Those files remain after exit. _state='ready' set at :531 is later overwritten by 'stopped' at :665, because _stopTree's waits are long, so the claim that the state can end as ready is unlikely. The file-leftover part holds. Exposure is limited to the same user (0600 file), and the offer is dead once that orcad is gone, because the device row is session-only.
votes.guard_or_evidence: No guard between OrcaService.sys.mjs:490 and :531. The only _shuttingDown checks in _spawnAndGate are at :434 and in _launch (:388,:392).

findings.title: Hand-off files from a crashed session are not cleared at start and are served to Theia before OrcaService runs
findings.description: Only _stopTree removes the bridge files web-pairing, orca-panes-dir and orcad-data-root. Nothing in _startSequence or _resolve clears them, and a crash skips the stop. powerbrowser.js starts OrcaService only after TheiaService.start settles, so the Theia frontend boots first. orca-pane-bundle.ts waitForPairing() takes the first offer handOff() returns, and handOff() does not check orcad's state. The frontend therefore boots its memoized pane bundle with the previous session's offer and bundle path. Per 67-03 (P65-17, A-7) the device row is session-only, so that offer is dead once the new orcad replaces the leftover. Before that happens, it authenticates to the leftover orcad that survived the crash, which OrcaService then kills. Expected result: Orca tabs come up in a pairing-lost state after every crash until the user presses Reconnect.
findings.scenario: PowerBrowser crashes. On relaunch the Theia frontend reads the old <bridge>/web-pairing at boot, bootstraps against the old orcad (still alive), and then OrcaService reaps that orcad and starts a new one whose device rows do not hold the old token. The Orca tabs show an unauthorized or pairing-lost state.
findings.evidence: powerbrowser.js:392 `TheiaService.start(browserElement)...finally(() => OrcaService.start()...)`; OrcaService.sys.mjs:106-115 `_startSequence` (resolve, preflight, reap, launch) has no bridge-file removal; theia/extensions/orca-panes/src/node/orca-panes-backend-module.ts:154-198 `handOff()` reads WEB_PAIRING_FILE with no orcad-state check; orca-pane-bundle.ts:102-108 `waitForPairing` returns the first offer, and `ready()` memoizes `this.booting ??= this.boot()`.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove the three bridge files at the start of _resolve, once _bridgeDir is known and before any spawn. Better, have handOff() refuse unless the offer was written after the current orcad's ready (for example, by a start nonce written beside it).
findings.preconditions: A previous session ended without a granted quit.

votes.reasoning: Nothing clears bridge files at start: _startSequence (:106-115), _resolve and TheiaService (_orcaBridgeDir, TheiaService.sys.mjs:789-797) never remove web-pairing. The bridge folder is the alias path plus '-bridge' (OrcaEnv.sys.mjs:292-296), which survives a crash. The frontend boots in onStart (orca-pane-bundle.ts:62-65), and its first waitForPairing poll is immediate (:102-108). The backend's handOff checks folder and file owner, mode, decoding and port (orca-panes-backend-module.ts:153-198) but not freshness, and the stale offer names the same port, so it passes. OrcaService starts only after TheiaService.start settles (powerbrowser.js:392), and the new offer appears only after the reap (up to killGraceMs) and a new ready line. At cold start the chrome state is 'starting' with restarting=false, so failureClassOf returns null (OrcaEnv.sys.mjs:504-518). The auto re-pair in orca-hosting-status.ts:288-296 fires only after 'restarting', 'could-not-start' or 'port-in-use' (:43), so it does not fire here. The step I cannot settle statically: whether the stale-offer client ends in a held unauthorized/pairing-lost state, or whether Orca's own client recovers. That depends on the frontend poll winning the race against the new writePrivateFile and on Orca's reconnect behaviour against the replacement orcad.
votes.guard_or_evidence: No freshness guard in handOff (orca-panes-backend-module.ts:153-198). Auto re-pair is limited to REPAIR_AFTER (orca-hosting-status.ts:43,288). The runtime step is the Orca client's behaviour after the replaced orcad refuses the old token.

findings.title: orcad crashes after ready are restarted without limit or backoff
findings.description: giveUpAttempts and the backoff apply only to consecutive failures inside one _launch call. Every successful ready ends that loop, so an orcad that reaches ready and then exits, from a crash bug, an agent-triggered fault or a bad restored session, is restarted by _supervise right away (attempt 1 has no sleep), indefinitely. _restartCount only grows. The state alternates between starting/restarting and ready and never reaches failed, so the failure page and Restart button never appear, and each cycle also kills and respawns orcad's subsystems.
findings.scenario: A restored session makes orcad throw 5 s after its ready line on every start. PowerBrowser spawns, gates and loses orcad about every 6-10 s for the whole session, burning CPU, and the user only sees a permanent 'restarting' state.
findings.evidence: OrcaService.sys.mjs:583-591 `this._restartCount += 1; ... await this._reapLeftover({ includeDaemon: false }); await this._launch();` with no limit; :387-392 `for (let attempt = 1; ; attempt += 1) { ... const result = await this._spawnAndGate(); if (result.ok || this._shuttingDown) { return; }` resets the attempt count on every ready.
findings.suggested_fix: Track exits within a time window (for example, N post-ready exits in M minutes) and switch to the failed state with a 'crashing repeatedly' row. Carry the backoff across supervise cycles instead of resetting it on ready.
findings.preconditions: orcad repeatedly exits soon after printing its ready line.

votes.reasoning: _launch's attempt counter and backoff are local to one call (:385-403) and it returns on the first ok (:392). _supervise (:574-595) has no cap or delay: it increments _restartCount, reaps and calls _launch again, and attempt 1 runs without a sleep. An orcad that reaches ready and then exits is therefore respawned indefinitely, and the state alternates between restarting and ready, never reaching failed. No pref or guard bounds _restartCount. The effect is CPU use and a permanent restarting state, which makes this a correctness or robustness issue rather than a security one.
votes.guard_or_evidence: No guard. OrcaService.sys.mjs:583-591 is unbounded, and :387-393 resets per call.

findings.title: A start rejected after orcad has started its detached daemon leaves that daemon untracked through quit
findings.description: orcad starts the detached terminal daemon early (orcad-entry.ts:75), well before it binds the WebSocket port and prints ready, and its own shutdown only disconnects from the daemon. Three OrcaService paths kill orcad through its process handle alone: the startup timeout (line 474), the loopback check (493) and the Node-version check (497). In none of them is the daemon recorded in _daemonPid or the state file. A port-in-use exit after daemon start does the same. At quit, _stopTree sees no live proc and _daemonPid is null, so the daemon is never ended. It lingers until its own idle shutdown, or indefinitely if it adopted or restored sessions. This breaks the RUN-05 goal that quit leaves nothing behind.
findings.scenario: orcad starts the daemon, then takes longer than 60 s to print ready on a slow first start. OrcaService SIGTERMs orcad, retries, and finally fails. The user quits PowerBrowser, and the orca-daemon-<nonce>.scope process is still running afterwards.
findings.evidence: OrcaService.sys.mjs:473-475 `if (outcome.timeout) { await endOwn(); return {...} }`, :492-499 `await endOwn(); return { ok: false, recoverable: false, ...}` before :503 `this._daemonPid = ready.daemonPid;`. endOwn (:427-433) is `PowerBrowserAPI.killProcess(proc, graceMs)` only. orca/src/main/orcad/orcad-daemon-supervision.ts:57-58 `stopOrcadDaemon() { await disconnectDaemon() }`.
findings.suggested_fix: Before endOwn on any failed gate, snapshot listProcessTree([proc.pid]) and kill the daemon rows the same way _endDaemon does. On the loopback and Node-version paths, also record ready.daemonPid so quit can reap it.
findings.preconditions: An orcad start fails after the daemon is spawned (timeout, loopback mismatch, Node below 24, or busy port).

votes.reasoning: orcad-entry.ts:72-81 starts the daemon early, in parallel with imports, and registers a cleanup that only disconnects (stopOrcadDaemon -> disconnectDaemon, orcad-daemon-supervision.ts:57-59). The pinned-port bind error comes from runtime/rpc/ws-transport.ts, which is reached after daemon start, whereas the instance lock is taken earlier in startOrcadWithHost. OrcaService's timeout (:473-475), loopback (:492-494) and Node-version (:496-498) rejections call endOwn, which is killProcess(proc) only (:427-433), before _daemonPid is set at :503. The port-code exit path (:477-486) also never records it. Retries reap with includeDaemon:false (:402). If every attempt fails, _stopTree finds the proc already exited and _daemonPid null, so _sameIdentity is false (:642) and the daemon is not in the tree (:643-644). _endDaemon(null, null, []) then does nothing. The state file was removed by the cold-start reap (:371-372) and never rewritten, so the next session's reap has no record of it either; that orcad simply adopts the daemon.
votes.guard_or_evidence: No guard. OrcaService.sys.mjs:474, :493, :497 and :485 return before :503-515 record the daemon. orcad-daemon-supervision.ts:57-59 is disconnect-only.

findings.title: The environment allowlist passes the SSH agent socket, the session bus and proxy settings to every skip-permissions agent
findings.description: ORCAD_ENV_ALLOWLIST correctly keeps POWERBROWSER_* secrets, NODE_OPTIONS and foreign ORCA_* names away from orcad. It deliberately passes SSH_AUTH_SOCK, DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS, DISPLAY/WAYLAND_DISPLAY and the HTTP(S)_PROXY values, which may hold user:password credentials, to orcad and through it to every agent, and agents run with skip-permissions (D-12). A prompt-injected agent can therefore use the user's loaded SSH keys and the unlocked Secret Service keyring over the session bus without any further step. A same-uid process can reach most of these anyway, so this is not a boundary crossing. It is worth recording that the allowlist is a hygiene filter, not a containment boundary for agents.
findings.scenario: A web page an agent reads tells it to run `ssh git@github.com` or `secret-tool lookup ...`. Both work from the agent's environment as passed by OrcaEnv.
findings.evidence: OrcaEnv.sys.mjs:37-63 `export const ORCAD_ENV_ALLOWLIST = Object.freeze([ "PATH", "HOME", ... "DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS", "SSH_AUTH_SOCK", "DISPLAY", "WAYLAND_DISPLAY", "HTTP_PROXY", "HTTPS_PROXY", ...`; :113-118 copies each into the orcad env.
findings.suggested_fix: Record the agent capability set in the threat model and docs. If containment is ever wanted, gate SSH_AUTH_SOCK and DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS behind a user setting.
findings.preconditions: An agent is steered by text it reads.

votes.reasoning: ORCAD_ENV_ALLOWLIST at OrcaEnv.sys.mjs:37-63 lists DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS (53), SSH_AUTH_SOCK (54), DISPLAY/WAYLAND_DISPLAY (55-56) and the six proxy names (57-62). buildOrcadEnv copies each one that is set (113-118). OrcaService.sys.mjs:412-422 passes that object as the whole orcad environment through spawnProcessExact. Per D-31, agents run on Orca's own terminal daemon, and upstream orca/src/main/daemon/daemon-launched-child-spawn.ts:94 spreads process.env into child spawns, so these values reach every agent. DECISIONS.md:79 (D-12) keeps skip-permissions on, so an agent steered by prompt injection can use the SSH agent and the session bus without a confirmation prompt. The finding states correctly that this is not a boundary crossing: any same-uid process already reaches the agent socket and the session bus, and the user deliberately passes them so agents can run git, ssh and GUI tools (comment at lines 32-35). Two things depend on the user's setup and cannot be settled statically: whether an ssh-agent with keys loaded and an unlocked Secret Service keyring exist at runtime. Neither changes the observation. D-12 accepts the risk, and that does not refute the finding. Info is the right severity: the allowlist is a hygiene filter, not a containment boundary.
votes.guard_or_evidence: OrcaEnv.sys.mjs:53-62 (allowlisted names), :113-118 (copy); OrcaService.sys.mjs:412,422 (spawn env = buildOrcadEnv output); DECISIONS.md:79 D-12 skip-permissions; DECISIONS.md:188 D-31 Orca terminal daemon used; orca/src/main/daemon/daemon-launched-child-spawn.ts:94 ...process.env to children. No guard strips these names.

findings.title: handOff returns the offer before orca-panes-dir exists, so a poll in that gap fails the pane bundle boot until the document reloads
findings.description: The protocol says handOff is undefined until both bridge files are written (orca-panes-protocol.ts:31). handOff checks only the web-pairing file. OrcaService._writeHandOff writes web-pairing first, then awaits pathExists(panesDir) and a whole second writePrivateFile before orca-panes-dir exists. If the frontend poll lands in that gap, the frontend gets the pairing and imports /orca-panes/pb-panes.js at once. bundleRootReal finds no orca-panes-dir and the route answers 404, so the boot fails at the load step. OrcaPaneBundle.ready caches the rejected promise and nothing resets it. OrcaHostingStatus.reconnect then does nothing: this.api is undefined, so it clears the client reason and returns. Its comment assumes the loader is still polling, but the loader has already failed. The chrome state is ready, so no failure class is set and no failure page appears. Orca tabs stay empty until the Theia document reloads.
findings.scenario: PowerBrowser launches and the Theia frontend starts polling handOff (1 s, 2 s, 4 s, then every 5 s). orcad prints its ready line. OrcaService writes web-pairing, and a handOff poll arrives before orca-panes-dir is renamed into place. The frontend loads pb-panes.js, gets a 404, and boot() rejects with failed set to 'load'. Every later bundle.ready() call rejects, and Reconnect does nothing.
findings.evidence: OrcaService.sys.mjs:552 writes the offer first: `await PowerBrowserProcesses.writePrivateFile(this._bridgeDir, OrcaEnv.ORCA_WEB_PAIRING_FILE, ...)`. Lines 559-567 run `pathExists(panesDir)` and then `writePrivateFile(..., ORCA_PANES_DIR_FILE, ...)`. orca-panes-backend-module.ts:169-198: handOff reads only WEB_PAIRING_FILE and returns `{ pairing }`. orca-panes-backend-module.ts:246-248: the route answers 404 when bundleRootReal() is undefined. orca-pane-bundle.ts:65-67: `return this.booting ??= this.boot();` and the boot catch at :94-97 rethrows. orca-hosting-status.ts:197-207: `if (this.api) {...}` then `// Not booted yet: the loader's own hand-off loop pairs with this offer.` and `this.setClientReason(undefined)`. pb-pane-mount.tsx:669 also memoises its own rejected `booting`.
findings.suggested_fix: Make handOff return undefined until orca-panes-dir passes readBridgeFile, which is what the protocol already states. Alternatively, write orca-panes-dir before web-pairing in _writeHandOff. Also clear OrcaPaneBundle.booting on a load or pairing failure, so that Reconnect, or the next handOff that succeeds, can retry the boot.
findings.preconditions: A handOff poll lands within the few milliseconds between the two bridge-file writes at an orcad start.

votes.reasoning: I traced every step. OrcaService._writeHandOff (OrcaService.sys.mjs:550-570) writes web-pairing, then awaits pathExists(panesDir), then calls writePrivateFile for orca-panes-dir. writePrivateFile (PowerBrowserAPI.sys.mjs:11071-11089) runs about seven IOUtils calls in sequence, so the gap is a few milliseconds of async work. handOff (orca-panes-backend-module.ts:154-198) lstats and reads only WEB_PAIRING_FILE, so it returns { pairing } during that gap. This breaks the protocol contract at orca-panes-protocol.ts:31 ('undefined until both bridge files are written'). OrcaPaneBundle.waitForPairing (orca-pane-bundle.ts:102-110) returns on the first pairing, and boot() goes straight to loadEntry. The route (backend :232-248) calls bundleRootReal(), which hits ENOENT on orca-panes-dir and returns undefined, so the route answers 404. The inline module script's import() rejects and dispatches LOAD_FAILED_EVENT, and boot() sets failed='load' and rethrows (:94-97). ready() memoises that rejected promise through `this.booting ??= this.boot()` (:66), and nothing resets booting. In OrcaHostingStatus.onStart the reject path calls settle, so bootSettled becomes true and the stuck-boot check (:298-301) never runs. this.api stays undefined, so runReconnect (:197-207) only clears the client reason. Once chrome reaches ready, failureClass is null, so no failure page is shown and the widget host stays empty (orca-pane-widget.tsx:110,142-146). The window exists only on a start where orca-panes-dir is absent, which is the normal case after a clean quit because _stopTree removes it (:630). On an orcad respawn the old file is still there. The poll landing in the window depends on timing, but that is the stated precondition, not an open runtime question. The race is narrow but its effect is visible to the user and lasts until the document reloads, so medium stands.
votes.guard_or_evidence: No guard. orca-panes-backend-module.ts:169-198 reads only web-pairing; OrcaService.sys.mjs:552 then :560-567; orca-pane-bundle.ts:66 `this.booting ??= this.boot()`; orca-hosting-status.ts:197-207 does nothing when api is undefined.

findings.title: The offer endpoint's port check compares the endpoint with a port read from the same file, so T-67-13's 'equal to orcad's port' check enforces nothing
findings.description: offerEndpointVerdict is meant to accept only orcad's own port (T-67-13: 'equal to orcad's port when known'). The port it compares with comes from offerPortOf(pairing), which parses the same untrusted text. The policy also accepts a bare offer that is not in URL form, and then no port is checked at all. Anyone who can write web-pairing can therefore point the hosted Orca client at any loopback port from 1024 to 32767, along with a publicKeyB64 of their choice. A listener on that port then serves the Orca runtime protocol to a client that renders inside the privileged Theia origin. The backend never learns the real orcad port independently, although chrome knows it (OrcaService._port).
findings.scenario: A same-user process, for example a prompt-injected agent with shell access in an Orca terminal, runs a fake runtime server on 127.0.0.1:4444. It writes web-pairing (0600, own uid) as either http://127.0.0.1:4444/web-index.html#pairing=<offer with endpoint ws://127.0.0.1:4444> or the bare base64 offer. The next frontend reload, Reconnect, or automatic re-pair after an orcad restart pairs the Theia-origin Orca client with the fake server, which sends the session data that Orca renders.
findings.evidence: offer-file-policy.ts:188-191: `const match = /^http:\/\/127\.0\.0\.1:([1-9][0-9]*)\//.exec(text.trim()); return match ? Number(match[1]) : undefined;`. offer-file-policy.ts:197: `(port !== undefined && n !== port)`. orca-panes-backend-module.ts:194: `offerEndpointVerdict(offer, offerPortOf(pairing))`. Both arguments derive from `pairing`, the file content.
findings.suggested_fix: Give the backend orcad's port from an independent source. One option is a separate chrome-written bridge file (orca-port), or the value TheiaService already passes through POWERBROWSER_ENV. Require the endpoint to equal that port, and refuse a bare offer that is not in URL form. Write the offer's own fields the same way and compare them, rather than trusting the text.
findings.preconditions: Write access to the 0700 bridge folder, which means a process of the same user.

votes.reasoning: The code is as described. offerPortOf (offer-file-policy.ts:188-191) parses the port from the same hand-off text, and handOff passes offerPortOf(pairing) as the expected port (orca-panes-backend-module.ts:194). The 'equal to orcad's port' clause is therefore only a consistency check inside one file. A bare offer gets no port comparison at all. The backend never learns OrcaService._port independently. The loopback-only and 1024-32767 part of T-67-13 (offer-file-policy.ts:195-197) is enforced. The precondition is effectively equivalent to holding the capability gained. Writing web-pairing needs a process running as the owner, because the folder must be 0700 and the file must be own-uid with no group or other bits (privateDirVerdict :57-70, offerFileVerdict :49-69). That process can already modify the user's PowerBrowser profile, the Orca install, or the Theia sidecar code, and so run code in the Theia origin directly. The hardening gap is real, but nothing crosses a privilege boundary.
votes.guard_or_evidence: The same-uid precondition comes from offerFileVerdict (offer-file-policy.ts:60-66) and privateDirVerdict (orca-panes-backend-module.ts:61-67). The port comparison is self-referential at orca-panes-backend-module.ts:194.

findings.title: Stale web-pairing and orca-panes-dir files are never cleared at start, on an unexpected orcad exit, on a failed launch, or when the new ready line has no offer, and handOff serves them as current
findings.description: The bridge files are removed only in _stopTree. A browser crash or kill leaves web-pairing behind. On Linux the bridge folder is under XDG_RUNTIME_DIR; on hosts without it, it falls back to HOME/.cache and survives reboots. Nothing removes the file at the next start or in _supervise. When a new ready line reports pairing.available false, _writeHandOff logs a line and leaves the previous start's offer in place. The backend has no generation or orcad-identity check, so it hands that stale credential to the frontend as this start's offer. Because orcad's token rows persist (see the next finding), the stale file is still a working runtime-scope credential, not dead data. This contradicts the OrcaEnv contract 'removed on stop' as a statement of the offer's lifetime.
findings.scenario: PowerBrowser is killed (OOM or SIGKILL), so _stopTree never runs. On the next launch, before orcad is ready, handOff returns the previous session's offer and the frontend pairs with it. Separately, an orcad restart whose ready line has pairing.available false (device_registry_unavailable) keeps serving the previous offer. Meanwhile the file holds a valid runtime token on disk for as long as the folder exists.
findings.evidence: OrcaService.sys.mjs:550-558: `if (offer) { ... writePrivateFile(... ORCA_WEB_PAIRING_FILE ...) } else { this._pushLog("orcad reported no pairing offer; Orca tabs cannot open."); }`, with no removal on the else branch. OrcaService.sys.mjs:630-632: the bridge files are removed only in _stopTree. _resolve, _reapLeftover, _supervise (574-595) and restart() (156-167) never remove them. OrcaEnv.sys.mjs:72-73: 'Written 0600 for the Theia backend only and removed on stop.'
findings.suggested_fix: Remove web-pairing and orca-panes-dir in _startSequence before the spawn, at the start of _supervise's relaunch, and on the no-offer branch of _writeHandOff. Optionally have the backend refuse an offer file whose mtime predates a chrome-written orcad-start marker.
findings.preconditions: A crash, kill, or a ready line with no offer. Reading the file requires the same uid.

votes.reasoning: The bridge files are removed only in _stopTree (OrcaService.sys.mjs:630-636). _resolve (:170-245), _reapLeftover (:359-377), _launch (:380-404), _supervise (:574-595) and restart() (:156-167) never remove web-pairing or orca-panes-dir. The else branch of _writeHandOff (:556-558) only logs, so a ready line with no offer leaves the previous offer in place. handOff has no generation or orcad-identity check (orca-panes-backend-module.ts:154-198), so it serves whatever file is there. On Linux without XDG_RUNTIME_DIR the folder falls back to $HOME/.cache/pb-orca-<hex>-bridge (OrcaEnv.sys.mjs:270-271, 292-295), which survives reboot. As traced under pairing-credentials-04, the token row the offer names is not revoked, so a stale file is still a usable credential and not dead data. Two things limit the impact. Reading the file requires the same uid. A frontend pairing with a stale offer mostly ends up connected to the same profile's orcad, which is a correctness and lifetime problem rather than an escalation. Low is defensible.
votes.guard_or_evidence: No removal path exists outside _stopTree (OrcaService.sys.mjs:630-636). The else branch at :556-558 has no unlink. OrcaEnv.sys.mjs:72-73 states 'removed on stop'.

findings.title: Every orcad start mints a new runtime-scope token row that is never revoked, so each offer PowerBrowser writes stays valid indefinitely
findings.description: PowerBrowser treats the offer as tied to one orcad start ('the session-only device row died with the old orcad'; D-36 cites P65-17). At the pin, the row that dies is only the ephemeral session-key fork. The legacy token row that the offer's deviceToken names survives. It is marked seen on first authentication, so it is no longer pending, and the next orcad start calls getOrCreatePendingDevice and creates another row with reach 'network'. Upstream removes token rows only through explicit user removal, and pruneIdleEphemeralDevices touches only ephemeral rows. Over months the profile's orca-devices.json accumulates one live full-runtime token per launch or orcad restart. Every web-pairing file, copy, or backup ever written stays a working credential against any later orcad on that profile. The pairing-containment check lists the registry as holder 5, but neither it nor any decision addresses the unbounded count or the lifetime.
findings.scenario: A user launches PowerBrowser daily for a year, and about 365 runtime-scope token rows accumulate. A web-pairing file left by a crash months ago, or found in a home-directory backup, still authenticates to today's orcad with full runtime control (terminals, files).
findings.evidence: orca/src/main/server/serve-pairing-readiness.ts: `rpc.createPairingOffer({ ..., scope: options.mobilePairing ? 'mobile' : 'runtime', grants: ... })` with no `reach`, so it defaults to 'network'. orca/src/main/runtime/device-registry.ts:96-107 reuses only `isPendingTokenRow(d)` (device-entry.ts:51-54: `device.lastSeenAt === 0 && ...`), otherwise `addDevice`. orca/src/main/runtime/ephemeral-device-rows.ts:20 prunes only `device.ephemeral === true`. orca-hosting-status.ts:20-22 states: 'the session-only device row died with the old orcad (P65-17, A-7)'.
findings.suggested_fix: At each orcad start (or stop), have PowerBrowser revoke the token row its previous offer named. pairedDeviceId is in the decoded offer, so chrome can record it in memory and remove it through orcad's device RPC or CLI after the new offer is written. Alternatively, request the offer with rotate so that pending rows are replaced, and remove seen PowerBrowser rows by name. Record the token's real lifetime in INTERNAL-APIS or DECISIONS.
findings.preconditions: Access to an old offer file or the registry, which requires the same uid or a backup copy of the profile.

votes.reasoning: PowerBrowser starts orcad with no rotate flag (buildOrcadArgs, OrcaEnv.sys.mjs:182). createPairingOffer (orca runtime-rpc-pairing.ts) then calls getOrCreatePendingDevice with reach defaulting to 'network'. getOrCreatePendingDevice (device-registry.ts:87-107) reuses a row only when isPendingTokenRow is true, which requires lastSeenAt === 0 (device-entry.ts:51-54); otherwise it calls addDevice. A token-authenticated socket reaches onReady, which calls updateLastSeenDeferred, and on first sighting that persists lastSeenAt immediately (mobile-socket-wiring.ts:245; device-registry.ts:252-265). The hosted client's first token authentication therefore takes the row out of the pending state, and the next orcad start mints a new row. Ephemeral pruning only touches rows with ephemeral === true (ephemeral-device-rows.ts:8-27). device-key-fork.ts:70 records forkedFrom, and device-entry.ts:35 documents that 'that row stays for its other holders', so the legacy token row survives the fork. The only removal is removeDevice, which an explicit user action triggers. This contradicts the 'session-only device row died with the old orcad' framing at orca-hosting-status.ts:20-22, which is true only of the ephemeral fork. Rows accumulate one per orcad start, and every old offer stays valid. The impact stays low. Exploiting it needs an old offer file or the registry itself, which means the same uid or a profile backup, and the backup already contains orca-devices.json with the tokens. orcad binds 127.0.0.1 only, so a token is usable only from the local host.
votes.guard_or_evidence: No revocation path. device-registry.ts:96-107 (pending-only reuse), mobile-socket-wiring.ts:245 (token row marked seen), ephemeral-device-rows.ts:8-27 (prunes only ephemeral rows), OrcaEnv.sys.mjs:182 (no rotate).

findings.title: orca-panes-dir, which picks the JavaScript executed in the privileged Theia origin, is read with less hardening than the offer and its target folder is never checked
findings.description: The offer path uses lstat, then an O_NOFOLLOW open with an fstat inode match. The orca-panes-dir path uses lstatSync and then readFileSync by path, which follows a symlink swapped in after the lstat. The folder named in the file is realpath'd and served with no check of its owner or mode, or of the files in it. Its pb-panes.js runs as a module script in the Theia document, which holds the backend token cookie and the Orca pairing. This makes it the most sensitive file in the bridge hand-off, and it gets the weakest check.
findings.scenario: An Orca root set through powerbrowser.orca.root points at a checkout in a group-writable shared folder. A second local user in that group replaces out/web/pb-panes/pb-panes.js, and the next PowerBrowser start runs that code in the Theia origin with the owner's backend access. Alternatively, a same-user process swaps orca-panes-dir for a symlink between the lstat and the read.
findings.evidence: orca-panes-backend-module.ts:126-130: `privateFileVerdict(fs.lstatSync(full), ...)` then `return fs.readFileSync(full, 'utf8')`. :215: `real: fs.realpathSync(readBridgeFile(this.bridgeDir, PANES_DIR_FILE))` with no owner or mode verdict on the folder. :251: `res.sendFile(path.relative(root, real), { root })`. Compare readNoFollow at :106-117, which the offer path uses.
findings.suggested_fix: Read orca-panes-dir through readNoFollow. Require the bundle folder realpath to be under the realpath of the Orca web client root that chrome resolved. Refuse a folder or entry file that is writable by group or other, or owned by another uid other than root.
findings.preconditions: A permissive or shared Orca install path, or a same-user writer.

votes.reasoning: The code is as described. readBridgeFile (orca-panes-backend-module.ts:120-131) calls lstatSync and then readFileSync by path, with no O_NOFOLLOW and no inode match, unlike readNoFollow (:106-117) on the offer path. bundleRootReal (:215) realpaths the named folder with no owner or mode check on it or its files, and the route serves files from it (:251). One detail is off: the bundle lives at out/web/assets/pb-panes (OrcaEnv.ORCA_PANES_DIR_REL), not out/web/pb-panes. Neither scenario gains a capability the attacker lacks. The symlink-swap race needs a writer to the 0700, own-uid bridge folder, which is a process running as the owner. The shared-checkout scenario needs write access to the same orcaRoot from which OrcaService already runs `${orcaRoot}/out/orcad/orcad.js` with Node as the user (OrcaService.sys.mjs:219-223, 422). That writer already gets code execution as the owner at the same trigger, the next PowerBrowser start, which is more than code in the Theia origin. Checking pb-panes.js more strictly than orcad.js would not close that path. This is a consistency observation, not an exploitable gap.
votes.guard_or_evidence: Equivalent capability: OrcaService.sys.mjs:223 `this._orcadMain = `${orcaRoot}/out/orcad/orcad.js`` is executed at :422 from the same root that holds out/web/assets/pb-panes. The bridge folder must be own-uid 0700 (privateDirVerdict, orca-panes-backend-module.ts:61-67).

findings.title: Third-party Orca renderer bundle runs in the sidecar's own origin with no CSP, so any Orca UI XSS reaches Theia's full RPC
findings.description: The Orca pane bundle (upstream Orca renderer code, re-pinned weekly under D-26) is loaded as a module script into the Theia document at http://127.0.0.1:<sidecar port>. The 67-02 gate admits its requests as same-origin by construction. Code in that document can call every authenticated Theia JSON-RPC service: filesystem read and write, terminal and process spawn, plugin install, and pb-orca-git. In Orca's own web build the renderer can only reach orcad. Here it renders untrusted remote text (GitHub/GitLab/Jira/Linear comments through CommentMarkdown with rehype-raw plus rehype-sanitize, markdown preview, Mermaid, ipynb), and it runs with Theia's privileges. No Content-Security-Policy is set on the Theia document (no CSP header or meta anywhere in theia/extensions or the browser app). Local code-execution safety therefore depends on every Orca sanitizer holding.
findings.scenario: An outside contributor posts a PR comment containing HTML that gets past Orca's rehype-sanitize schema (an upstream regression at a weekly re-pin, or a gap in a schema extension such as the file-link allowance at CommentMarkdown.tsx:217). The user opens the PR in an Orca pane. The script runs at the sidecar origin, opens a Theia terminal over the authenticated socket, and runs commands as the user.
findings.evidence: orca-pane-bundle.ts:135-145: `const url = new URL(ORCA_PANES_ROUTE_PREFIX + ORCA_PANES_ENTRY, document.baseURI).href; ... script.textContent = [`import(${JSON.stringify(url)})...`]; document.head.appendChild(script);` ; orca-panes-backend-module.ts:227-251 serves that bundle from the gated `/orca-panes/` route on the same origin; orca/src/renderer/src/components/sidebar/CommentMarkdown.tsx:231-232 `// GitHub comments use raw HTML; parse it then sanitize before rendering. const rehypePlugins = [rehypeRaw, [rehypeSanitize, commentMarkdownSanitizeSchema]]`. 67-02-SUMMARY: pane-bundle requests are 'same-origin ... -> 200'.
findings.suggested_fix: Set a strict CSP on the Theia document (script-src 'self' with the inline boot replaced by a hashed or nonce'd script, no unsafe-eval where Monaco allows it, object-src 'none'). Consider hosting the Orca pane bundle in a separate origin or frame that reaches only orcad and a narrow postMessage bridge, so an Orca-side XSS does not get the Theia RPC. At minimum, add a re-pin check that diffs Orca's sanitize schemas and raw-HTML sinks.
findings.preconditions: An HTML-injection flaw in Orca's renderer, present at the pinned tag, reachable from content an attacker can author (a PR, issue or comment the user views in an Orca pane).

votes.reasoning: The structure is as described. orca-pane-bundle.ts:135-145 loads ORCA_PANES_ROUTE_PREFIX+ORCA_PANES_ENTRY as a module script into the Theia document. orca-panes-backend-module.ts:225-252 serves it from configure(), behind the token gate, on the same origin. No CSP header or meta exists in theia/extensions or theia/applications sources. The only CSP strings in the built backend are express/send `default-src 'none'` on error responses. The only PB CSP is on chrome powerbrowser.xhtml:30. The bundle (orca-overlay/files/src/renderer/src/pb/pb-pane-mount.tsx, pb-side-mounts.tsx) mounts NativeChatView, Sidebar, RightSidebar and CheckRunDetailsPanel, and these use CommentMarkdown, which runs rehypeRaw plus rehypeSanitize (CommentMarkdown.tsx:231-232). The impact claim overstates what PB adds. The same bundle receives orcad's pairing (orca-pane-bundle.ts:85-86). Under D-31, Orca terminals run on Orca's own daemon again (DECISIONS.md:11-16, 66-67). An Orca renderer XSS therefore already reaches shell execution through orcad in upstream Orca's web build and inside PB alike. Theia RPC is a second path to a capability class the XSS already has, not a new privilege boundary. The whole chain also depends on a hypothetical sanitizer bypass. This is a real defence-in-depth gap (no CSP on a document that runs third-party code against untrusted content), but it is low rather than medium.
votes.guard_or_evidence: No CSP: grep over theia/extensions and theia/applications finds no Content-Security-Policy outside express error handlers. Equivalent existing capability: the orcad pairing is handed to the bundle at orca-pane-bundle.ts:85-86; Orca's terminal daemon is in use per DECISIONS.md D-31 (lines 11-16, 66-67).

findings.title: pb-orca-git git reads do not disable lazy fetch or prompts, and a timeout kills only git and leaves its fetch children running
findings.description: runGit removes GIT_* from the environment and passes only `-c core.fsmonitor=false`. It does not set GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1, GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 or protocol.allow restrictions, and it does not drop SSH_ASKPASS. In a partial-clone (promisor) worktree, `git cat-file blob -- <oid>:<path>` for a missing tree or blob starts a lazy `git fetch` against the repository's configured remote. That fetch uses repository-level `core.sshCommand`, `remote.<n>.uploadpack` (which runs locally for a file/local remote), credential helpers and askpass. execFile's 10 s timeout sends SIGTERM to the git process only, so the spawned fetch, ssh or remote-helper children keep running. The header comment says the read has 'no textconv or filter, fsmonitor off' and every GIT_* name removed, but lazy fetch is not covered.
findings.scenario: The user adds an extracted project archive that contains a .git directory as an Orca folder workspace (same owner, so safe.directory passes). Its .git/config sets `extensions.partialClone=origin`, `remote.origin.promisor=true`, `remote.origin.url=/tmp/x` and `remote.origin.uploadpack=sh -c 'payload' #`. Orca shows a commit diff, and PowerBrowser's router opens it as a Theia diff. readBlob runs cat-file, the missing object starts a fetch, and the uploadpack command runs. In an ordinary blob:none clone, opening a historical diff instead makes a network fetch that can show a KDE askpass dialog and leaves orphaned fetch processes after the timeout.
findings.evidence: orca-workspace-backend-module.ts:27-33 `execFile('git', args, { env: withoutGitVars(process.env), encoding: 'buffer', maxBuffer: ORCA_GIT_MAX_BYTES, timeout: ORCA_GIT_TIMEOUT_MS, windowsHide: true }` ; orca-git-protocol.ts:46 `return ['-c', 'core.fsmonitor=false', '-C', root, 'cat-file', 'blob', '--', `${rev}:${relativePath}`];` Source: OrcaEditorRouter.uriOfRoute -> OrcaGitResourceResolver.resolve -> OrcaGitService.readBlob -> runGit.
findings.suggested_fix: Set GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1, GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 and GIT_ASKPASS/SSH_ASKPASS to empty or `true` in the child env. Add `-c protocol.allow=never` (as Orca's own plugin-git-arguments.ts does). Spawn git detached in its own process group and kill the group on timeout.
findings.preconditions: A repository whose .git/config the attacker controls (archive or shared directory, not an ordinary clone), or a partial clone for the network and leak variant. Orca's own git status and diff calls on the same repository do not disable fsmonitor either, so PowerBrowser adds little new exposure for a hostile config.

votes.reasoning: The code is as described. runGit (orca-workspace-backend-module.ts:25-42) removes GIT_* through withoutGitVars (orca-git-protocol.ts:50-52). It adds only -c core.fsmonitor=false (orca-git-protocol.ts:46). It does not set GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH or GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT, which the GIT_* filter would strip anyway, and it keeps SSH_ASKPASS. The 10 s execFile timeout signals only the direct git child. Inputs come from Orca records through OrcaEditorRouter and OrcaGitResourceResolver. Git triggers a promisor lazy fetch for a missing blob in a partial clone, and protocol.file.allow=user permits it because GIT_PROTOCOL_FROM_USER is unset. The hostile-config RCE variant needs an attacker-controlled .git/config in a user-owned repository, and Orca's own git status/diff calls in that worktree already run any hostile core.fsmonitor, so it is close to equivalent to holding the capability. The finding concedes this. The remaining effect is real but minor: an unwanted network fetch, an askpass dialog, and possibly orphaned processes. One runtime step cannot be settled statically: whether git's lazy-fetch child (promisor-remote fetch_objects, spawned without clean_on_exit as I read it) survives SIGTERM to the parent cat-file. That step decides the orphan claim.
votes.guard_or_evidence: Unsettled step: whether the lazy-fetch child survives SIGTERM to the parent cat-file. Code: orca-workspace-backend-module.ts:27-33 and orca-git-protocol.ts:46,50-52. Partial mitigation of the RCE variant: Orca itself runs git in the same worktree without disabling fsmonitor, so a hostile config already executes there.

findings.title: A planted POWERBROWSER_TOKEN cookie with a longer path shadows the real token, and the gate reads only the first match
findings.description: Cookies are not port-isolated. Any script on any http://127.0.0.1:<port> origin, including orcad's own web client (which v1.7 loads in stock windows and web tabs), can set a non-HttpOnly cookie named POWERBROWSER_TOKEN with a more specific path such as /socket.io/ or /orca-panes/. HttpOnly on the real cookie prevents overwriting it but not adding a distinct-path cookie. Browsers list longer-path cookies first. getTokenFromCookie returns the first POWERBROWSER_TOKEN entry, so the gate checks the planted value and returns 403 for every request under that path. The chrome's strip observer removes POWERBROWSER_TOKEN entries only on requests it does not allow; it leaves sidecar-origin requests unchanged. The impact is availability only: a valid token cannot be fixed or learned this way.
findings.scenario: Script on a page at 127.0.0.1:26768 (orcad's client, through an Orca XSS) or on another local server the user visits runs `document.cookie = 'POWERBROWSER_TOKEN=x; path=/socket.io/'`. The next Theia WebSocket handshake carries `POWERBROWSER_TOKEN=x; POWERBROWSER_TOKEN=<real>`. allowWsUpgrade reads `x` and refuses, the Theia frontend cannot connect, and this lasts until the cookie is cleared.
findings.evidence: token-gate-backend-contribution.ts:214-221 `for (const part of header.split(';')) { ... if (name === POWERBROWSER_TOKEN_COOKIE_NAME) { return part.slice(eq + 1).trim(); } }` ; PowerBrowserAPI.sys.mjs:6359 `if (channel.URI.host !== "127.0.0.1" || tokenCookieAllowed(channel)) { return; }` (allowed requests are passed through unchanged).
findings.suggested_fix: Accept the request if any POWERBROWSER_TOKEN value in the header validates, comparing each value in constant time. Alternatively, in the http-on-modify-request observer, rewrite the Cookie header on allowed sidecar requests to carry only the chrome-set token.
findings.preconditions: Script execution on some http://127.0.0.1:<port> origin in the user's profile (orcad's page, or any local server the user browses to in a stock window).

votes.reasoning: The real cookie is set non-Secure, HttpOnly, host 127.0.0.1, path / (TheiaService.sys.mjs:1092-1097 → PowerBrowserAPI.sys.mjs:555-568). Because it is not Secure, the 'leave secure cookies alone' rule does not stop a shadowing cookie. Gecko's HttpOnly overwrite refusal applies only to an exact name/host/path match, so a script-set POWERBROWSER_TOKEN with path=/socket.io/ is a distinct cookie. Cookies are not port-scoped, so any 127.0.0.1:<port> page in the same jar can plant it. Gecko orders longer paths first. getTokenFromCookie (token-gate-backend-contribution.ts:214-223) returns the first match, and allowWsUpgrade (198-207) and gate (163-171) then refuse with 403. The strip observer (PowerBrowserAPI.sys.mjs:6359) returns early for allowed sidecar requests and leaves both entries in place. The impact is availability only. One step depends on Gecko runtime cookie-store behaviour that I cannot settle statically: whether the script-set non-HttpOnly cookie with a longer path is accepted alongside the HttpOnly one and sent first. Precondition: script on some loopback origin (an Orca XSS or a local server the user browses).
votes.guard_or_evidence: Unsettled step: Gecko's acceptance and ordering of a same-name, longer-path, non-HttpOnly cookie next to the HttpOnly path=/ cookie. First-match read: token-gate-backend-contribution.ts:214-223. Real cookie attributes: PowerBrowserAPI.sys.mjs:555-568 (aIsSecure false), TheiaService.sys.mjs:1092-1097 (path '/').

findings.title: The served Orca bundle directory is not checked for ownership or mode, but its files run as script in the sidecar origin
findings.description: bundleRootReal checks that the bridge folder and the orca-panes-dir pointer file are private, then uses realpathSync on whatever directory the pointer names and serves any regular file under it. Neither that directory nor its parents are checked for owner or group/other write bits. Every file served there is loaded as a module into the Theia document (see the pane-bundle finding), so whoever can write into that directory can run code with the token-holding origin. The bridge files get the private-file rule; the code they point at does not.
findings.scenario: PowerBrowser is installed or built in a location where another local user has write access (for example a group-writable checkout or a shared /opt tree with lax permissions). That user replaces pb-panes.js. At the next launch it runs in the victim's Theia origin with full Theia RPC.
findings.evidence: orca-panes-backend-module.ts:215 `this.bundleRoot = { mtimeMs, real: fs.realpathSync(readBridgeFile(this.bridgeDir, PANES_DIR_FILE)) };` and :246-251 `if (!root || !real || !real.startsWith(root + path.sep) || !fs.statSync(real).isFile()) {...} res.sendFile(path.relative(root, real), { root });` with no ownership or mode check of root.
findings.suggested_fix: Apply privateDirVerdict-style checks (owned by the current uid or root, no group or other write bit) to the bundle root and each ancestor, or verify a hash manifest written at build time before serving the entry.
findings.preconditions: A bundle directory, or one of its ancestors, writable by another local user.

votes.reasoning: The code matches the description: bundleRootReal realpaths the pointed-to directory without checking its owner or mode (orca-panes-backend-module.ts:215, 246-251). The precondition, however, is equivalent to the capability gained. The pointer always names `${orcaRoot}/out/web/assets/pb-panes` (OrcaService.sys.mjs:559, 567), with orcaRoot being `${appDir}/orca` beside the PB binary or the powerbrowser.orca.root pref (OrcaService.sys.mjs:218-224). That same tree holds out/orcad/orcad.js, which PB runs with node as the user, and out/web, which orcad serves as its own web client. Anyone who can write into the bundle directory or an ancestor can already replace orcad.js and get code execution as the user without going through the Theia origin. The described scenarios are a group-writable checkout or a lax /opt tree, and in both the whole Orca install tree is writable.
votes.guard_or_evidence: OrcaService.sys.mjs:218-224 (orcaRoot, orcadMain = ${orcaRoot}/out/orcad/orcad.js, webClientRoot = ${orcaRoot}/out/web) and :559 (panesDir = ${webClientRoot}/assets/pb-panes): the served directory sits inside the tree whose orcad.js PB executes as the user, so write access to it is already code execution.

findings.title: OrcaGitService accepts any repository on disk as a root; the Orca-roots restriction exists only in the frontend
findings.description: The backend comment says every input is validated whatever the frontend checked. validateRoot only requires an absolute, realpath-stable repository toplevel. It never checks that the root is an Orca worktree or a PowerBrowser-owned root. That restriction exists only in OrcaGitResourceResolver.trustedRoots. OrcaEditorRouter.routeHelpers also calls resolveHead with the Orca-supplied worktreePath directly, without the trusted-root check. Any code holding the authenticated socket (the Theia frontend, including the Orca bundle running in the same document) can therefore read any blob from the history or index of any git repository the user can read. The same caller already has Theia's FileSystem service, so the extra capability is convenient access to historical or deleted blobs. This is recorded because the code comment overstates the backend's checks.
findings.scenario: Script in the Theia document calls readBlob('/home/user/.password-store', 'secret.gpg', '<old commit oid>'), or reads a credential file deleted from a dotfiles repository's history.
findings.evidence: orca-workspace-backend-module.ts:55-56 `const refusal = specRefusal(relativePath, rev) ?? await validateRoot(root, ROOT_DEPS);` ; orca-git-protocol.ts:61-70 validateRoot checks shape, realpath and toplevel only; orca-editor-routes.ts:400 `return { headOid: await this.git.resolveHead(file.worktreePath) };`
findings.suggested_fix: Either keep a backend-side set of allowed roots (fed from the same Orca store snapshot or the persisted owned roots) or correct the comment so it states that the frontend is the trust boundary.

The Orca-root restriction is in the frontend OrcaGitResourceResolver.trustedRoots/resolve (orca-git-resource.ts:55-70). routeHelpers calls resolveHead(file.worktreePath) directly (orca-editor-routes.ts:400).
