findings.title: A restored Orca tab cannot be closed while the pane bundle has failed or never finishes booting
findings.description: onCloseRequest never disposes a hosted (non-page) widget itself. It forwards the close to Orca. When the bundle boot failed (bundle.failed set), it logs and returns. When the boot is still pending (waitForPairing loops forever while orcad has not written the offer), ready() never resolves and the close is dropped. The observer, the only other path that disposes these widgets (disposeFromStore), starts only after ready() resolves. So every Orca tab that Theia's layout restorer recreated stays open and cannot be closed. It is saved into the layout again and comes back at every launch.
findings.scenario: The user had pb-orca:term1 and pb-orca:chat1 open. At the next launch the bundle fails at the identity or load step (for example a bundle/React version drift), or orcad never becomes ready. Theia restores both tabs. The user clicks X, or presses Ctrl+Shift+W (now bound to CLOSE_TAB by this change), on each tab. Nothing happens beyond a console line, and the tabs come back on every relaunch until Orca boots again.
findings.suggested_fix: When the bundle has failed, or Orca's store does not hold the pane (closePane finds no unified tab), dispose the widget locally. Also give the pending boot a bound: a close requested while ready() is unresolved past a timeout should dispose the tab. The Orca pane, if it exists, is re-adopted by key on the next list.
findings.preconditions: The bundle boot fails or orcad never writes the pairing offer, while Theia's stored layout contains hosted Orca tabs.

votes.reasoning: orca-pane-widget.tsx:159-171 disposes only tabless (page) widgets. For a hosted widget it returns early when bundle.failed is set, and otherwise chains on bundle.ready(). orca-pane-bundle.ts:66 caches the boot promise in `booting ??=`, and nothing resets it, so after a failed step bundle.failed stays set for the rest of the session. waitForPairing (bundle.ts:102-110) is an unbounded loop that exits only when an offer arrives, so while orcad has written no offer ready() stays pending and closePane is never sent. The only other dispose path is disposeFromStore, called from observer.ts:214 inside start(), and start() runs only after ready() resolves (observer.ts:105). The widget factory (frontend-module.ts:171-178) builds the widget from the replayed options without depending on the bundle, so Theia's layout restorer recreates these tabs, and storeLayout saves them again. Every close route in Theia (X, Close Tab, Close All) ends in onCloseRequest. In the pending-offer case the close does take effect later if orcad recovers, but in the failed-boot case the tab cannot be closed for the whole session and returns at every launch.
votes.guard_or_evidence: orca-pane-widget.tsx:165-170 (early return when failed, ready() chain otherwise); orca-pane-bundle.ts:66 (cached boot promise, no reset); orca-pane-bundle.ts:102-110 (unbounded poll); orca-pane-observer.ts:105 and :214 (disposeFromStore reachable only after ready()). No guard found.

findings.title: An Orca store activation of any origin brings an agent web tab forward and gives it keyboard focus
findings.description: revealBrowserTabs runs on every pane list. It calls shell.activateWidget, which moves keyboard focus, for each browser page whose `active` flag went from false to true. The record's `active` is Orca's group activeTabId, so a user click in Orca's sidebar and a change made by an agent through Orca's runtime look the same. Orca exposes browser.tabSwitch, browser.focus and terminal.focus as runtime RPCs to agents. The rest of this extension keeps agent actions from taking focus (P64-10: "an agent opening a pane must not take focus"; D-57). This path is the exception, and the tab it focuses is an agent-controlled page.
findings.scenario: A prompt-injected agent with an Orca browser page switches Orca's active tab to that page, or toggles another tab and back, while the user is typing in a Theia editor or a hosted terminal. The PowerBrowser web tab is activated and receives focus. The user's next keystrokes (a command, a passphrase typed at a terminal prompt) go to a page the agent drives and can read through its own browser tools.
findings.suggested_fix: Reveal without focus: use shell.revealWidget, or activate only when Theia's current focus is already inside the Orca sidebar view that made the selection. Alternatively, have the bundle report whether the activation came from a user gesture in a hosted view and reveal only those.
findings.preconditions: An Orca agent can change the paired web client's store activeTabId for a browser row. Whether browser.tabSwitch or browser.focus does this for PB-hosted rows is not settled statically.

votes.reasoning: Most of the path checks out. revealBrowserTabs (observer.ts:262-264) calls shell.activateWidget, which moves focus, for each page that createRevealTracker (orca-browser-dispatch.ts:203-216) reports as having turned from inactive to active. The tracker cannot tell a user selection from any other change to the store. An agent controls the input: browser.tabSwitch is a 'workspace'-permission RPC (orca/src/main/runtime/rpc/methods/browser-core.ts:120-125) that takes a page id and focus:true from the caller. For a client-registered page, browser-tab-queries.ts:97-140 calls registry.activatePage and publishSwitchedBrowserSessionTab, which republishes the session tabs and, when focus is true, calls markHeadlessBrowserSessionTabActive with focusesHost (browser-tab-create-publication.ts:158-176). One step cannot be settled statically. That step is whether that republish or focus marker changes the paired pane client's group activeTabId for the row PowerBrowser itself added under D-34 (overlay pb-pane-mount.tsx:828 derives `active` from it). D-34 says 'Selecting the row in Orca's store brings the PowerBrowser web tab forward (P66-09)', so the owner intended reveal on selection. That decision does not separate user selections from agent ones, and it does not accept the agent case.
votes.guard_or_evidence: Unsettled step: whether Orca's runtime activatePage or the focusesHost marker sets the pane client's store activeTabId for a PB-added browser row (orca/src/main/runtime/browser-tab-create-publication.ts:162-176 through to the paired client). No guard in revealBrowserTabs or createRevealTracker separates an agent-caused activation from a user one.

findings.title: The launch prune treats an unreadable or corrupt setups.json as naming nothing, so tombstoned pb-orca names a Setup still uses are released and minted again
findings.description: referencedTabUris() catches any read error of setups.json and returns an empty set for it, and uses parseSetupStore(...).setups even when parsed.ok is false. OrcaPaneNameMap.prune then drops every tombstone that the session snapshot does not name. SetupsService's own loader says read failures happen in a mid-save race. Once a tombstone is pruned, mintName can issue that name to a different Orca pane, and a saved Setup that names pb-orca:<name> then opens the wrong pane in its slot. This is the case T-65-13 says is mitigated: "never reissued while a Setup or the session names them".
findings.scenario: A Setup 'Review' contains pb-orca:chat2, whose Orca chat was closed, so chat2 is a tombstone. At launch, setups.json is caught mid-write by another window, or is unparseable after a partial write. prune() drops the chat2 tombstone. The user starts a new Orca chat, and planPanes mints chat2 for it. Restoring 'Review' later opens the new, unrelated chat as the Setup's chat2 tab.
findings.suggested_fix: Return a tri-state from referencedTabUris: distinguish 'file absent' (empty is correct) from 'read failed' or 'parse not ok', and skip the prune when the reference set is unknown. A tombstone left in place an extra launch costs nothing.
findings.preconditions: A read failure or a not-ok parse of setups.json at frontend start, while a tombstoned name is referenced only by a saved Setup.

votes.reasoning: setups-service.ts:1419-1432 catches a read failure and uses an empty list. parseSetupStore (setups-service.ts:348-373) returns {ok:false, setups:[]} for an unparseable file, and referencedTabUris uses .setups without checking ok. The prune contribution (orca-pane-name-map.ts:147-150) runs on onStart and passes that set to prune (name-map.ts:124-133), which deletes every tombstone not named by the set. After that the name is free, because mintName (orca-pane-routes.ts:81-88) skips only the names in the taken set, which comes from the map. A Setup that later reads correctly then resolves pb-orca:<name> through the new live entry (name-map.ts:203-209). This defeats the mitigation stated in T-65-13. The precondition is narrow. The writes go through a single fileService.write, which the code comment at setups-service.ts:628 describes as atomic to readers. A corrupt file that stays corrupt also makes the Setup itself unrestorable. So the harm needs a transient read failure, or a corrupt file that is later repaired.
votes.guard_or_evidence: setups-service.ts:1421-1424 (catch gives an empty list, parsed.ok not checked); orca-pane-name-map.ts:125-129 (unconditional delete of unreferenced tombstones). No guard found. The likelihood is limited by single-write saves (setups-service.ts:628-630).

findings.title: A user's existing custom mode named "Orca" is silently dropped on upgrade and erased on the next mode save
findings.description: v1.7 adds a shipped mode labelled 'Orca'. parseModeStore skips any stored custom row whose name matches a shipped label (`continue`), without adding it to badNames, so no notice is shown. The next saveCustom writes `[...this.lastGoodCustoms, row]`, which removes the user's row from storage permanently. A persisted active id of custom-orca then resolves to Browsing.
findings.scenario: Before v1.7 the user saved a custom mode named 'Orca' (or 'orca') with their own panel and view layout. After the upgrade it no longer appears, and the app opens in Browsing. When the user saves any other custom mode, the old row is deleted from the mode store without notice.
findings.suggested_fix: Migrate a colliding legacy row instead of dropping it: rename it (for example 'Orca (custom)'), or keep it under its custom-<slug> id with a distinct label, and report it through the existing badNames notice path.
findings.preconditions: A custom mode named 'Orca' was saved before v1.7.

votes.reasoning: mode-service.ts:216-220 skips a stored custom row whose name matches a shipped label, case-insensitively, with `continue` and does not add it to badNames. No notice is shown for it. saveCustom (mode-service.ts:514-516) writes `[...this.lastGoodCustoms, row]`, so the skipped row is removed from the file on the next save. git log shows the 'Orca' shipped label was added in b0ded1ab (2026-11-10, phase 64-03), inside v1.7, so a pre-v1.7 custom mode named 'Orca' would collide. Impact is limited because, according to project memory, no public release exists yet, so only pre-release profiles can hold such a row.
votes.guard_or_evidence: mode-service.ts:216-220 (silent skip); mode-service.ts:514-516 (rewrite from lastGoodCustoms); mode-descriptors.ts:57,66 (Orca label added in b0ded1ab). No migration or notice path found.

findings.title: pb-orca:creating opens the worktree creation surface when no creation is pending
findings.description: ORCA_PAGE_ROUTES marks the creating page whilePendingCreation, and docs/URI-SCHEMES.md says it is "open only while an Orca worktree creation is pending". The restore opener nevertheless creates a page:creation widget for the name 'creating' whenever the URI is opened: typed in the address bar, opened from a Setup or session restore, or recreated by Theia's layout restorer, since page widgets are never disposed from a list. Nothing reads whilePendingCreation. Only OrcaSidePanelSync closes the tab, and only on a pending-to-not-pending transition.
findings.scenario: A Setup saved while a creation was pending contains pb-orca:creating. Restoring it, or a relaunch with that tab in the layout, mounts Orca's CreationMount with no pending creation. The tab stays until the user closes it, because no creationChanged transition occurs.
findings.suggested_fix: In widgetFor, refuse the whilePendingCreation route unless the side-panel sync reports pendingCreation. Close a layout-restored page:creation widget at start when the store reports no pending creation.
findings.preconditions: The pb-orca:creating URI is opened, or present in a Setup, session or layout, while no creation is pending.

votes.reasoning: whilePendingCreation appears only in its type and route declaration (orca-pane-routes.ts:56,68) and is read nowhere in theia/. OrcaPaneRestoreOpenHandler.widgetFor (orca-pane-name-map.ts:190-195) creates a page:creation widget for 'creating' on any open, with no pending-creation check. Page widgets are tabless, are excluded from restoredWidgets (observer.ts restoredWidgets filters on tabId), and are skipped in plan.dispose (observer.ts:208-209), so the observer never closes them. OrcaSidePanelSync.onActiveView (side-panel-sync.ts:219-228) closes the tab only on a transition from pending to not pending. Its initial pendingCreation is false (line 108), so a not-pending state at startup produces no close. The result contradicts docs/URI-SCHEMES.md:211. The effect is a stale creation surface that the user can still close, since tabless widgets do dispose on close.
votes.guard_or_evidence: orca-pane-name-map.ts:191-195 (no pending check); orca-side-panel-sync.ts:221-228 (closes only when creationChanged and the creation is not pending); whilePendingCreation has no reader.

findings.title: Layout-restored OrcaPaneOptions are not validated; a prototype-key kind reaches Orca's title lookup
findings.description: The widget factory accepts the construction options Theia's layout restorer replays from profile shell state, with no type or route check. The name map validates its own entries (entryOf, a name regex), but the layout path skips that check. For a tabless widget, options.kind goes straight to the bundle's viewTitle, which indexes a plain object literal with `TITLES[kind]?.()`. A kind such as 'constructor' calls Object() and returns {}, which is truthy and is assigned to title.label and title.caption as a non-string. The kind is also written into a data-pb-orca-pane attribute that the scoped Orca stylesheet selects on, and passed to mountPane.
findings.scenario: A tampered or version-drifted powerbrowser-shell-state.json layout contains a powerbrowser.orca-pane widget with options {name:'x', kind:'constructor', tabId:''}. On restore the widget sets title.label to an object. Theia's tab renderer and hover then receive a non-string label and caption, which can break rendering of that dock tab bar.
findings.evidence:
orca-panes-frontend-module.ts:173-177: `createWidget: (options: OrcaPaneOptions) => { ... child.bind(OrcaPaneWidgetOptions).toConstantValue(options); ...}`
orca-pane-widget.tsx:87-91: `const title = (api as unknown as { viewTitle(kind: string): string }).viewTitle(this.options.kind); if (title && !this.isDisposed) { this.setRecordTitle(title, ''); }`
pb-workspace-api.ts:225-227: `return TITLES[kind]?.() ?? ''`
findings.suggested_fix: In createWidget, validate the options against the route tables: kind must be a hosted ORCA_PANE_ROUTES key, or a PAGE_WORDS value with an empty tabId; name must match /^[a-z]+\d*$/; all ids must be strings. Refuse anything else, and have setRecordTitle accept only strings. In the overlay, look up TITLES with an own-property check.
findings.preconditions: Write access to the profile's shell-state file (same local user), or layout data from an incompatible build.

votes.reasoning: The described code behaviour is accurate. The factory (orca-panes-frontend-module.ts:171-178) binds the replayed options without validation. For a tabless widget, init (orca-pane-widget.tsx:85-92) passes options.kind to viewTitle, and viewTitle (orca-overlay/files/src/renderer/src/pb/pb-workspace-api.ts:225-227) indexes a plain object literal, so 'constructor' returns Object() = {}, which is truthy. It fails check (4). The only actor who can supply such a kind is one with write access to the same user's profile shell state, and that actor can already damage or replace the UI and the profile directly. Version drift from another build does not trigger it: drifted kinds are real route strings such as 'page:x', which return undefined and then ''. The result is self-inflicted rendering damage, with no boundary crossed. As hardening, an own-property check in viewTitle or route validation in the factory is still reasonable.
votes.guard_or_evidence: Precondition is equivalent to the capability: write access to the same user's profile shell state. Drift does not produce prototype keys, because pb-workspace-api.ts:226 returns '' for any non-prototype unknown kind.

findings.title: Wrapper leaks an Orca pane when the pane-key lookup fails after the pane was created, or when a signal arrives during the synchronous CLI phase
findings.description: createPane creates the terminal first, then may call `terminal show` (errors swallowed) and `terminal list`. The `list` call is not inside a try block, so a timeout, non-zero exit or non-JSON output throws a raw execFileSync/JSON error that has no `.pane` property. main() closes a half-created pane only when `e?.pane?.handle` is set (line 192), so in this path the pane is never closed. The same happens when `terminal create` times out after orcad has already created the terminal, or when its output does not parse. Separately, the SIGINT/SIGTERM/SIGHUP handlers are installed only after spawn (line 205). A SIGTERM during the up-to-60 s synchronous CLI phase therefore kills the wrapper with the default action, and a pane that was already created is left behind. Each leaked pane is a 'Claude Code' Orca terminal tab running `cat` with no agent in it, and it stays until orcad restarts.
findings.scenario: orcad is under load. `terminal create` returns a handle but no paneKey, `terminal show` fails, and `terminal list` exceeds the 20 s timeout. The ETIMEDOUT error reaches main() without `.pane`. The wrapper logs 'terminal create failed' and runs claude unwrapped. The created pane is never closed, and the user sees an orphan 'Claude Code' tab in Orca. A user who cancels the extension session during that window (SIGTERM to the wrapper) gets the same orphan pane.
findings.evidence: claude-wrapper.mjs:151-152 `if (!pane.paneKey) { const listed = runCli(dataRoot, ['terminal', 'list'], env);` (no try, no pane attached to the thrown error); :190-193 `try { pane = createPane(...) } catch (e) { if (e?.pane?.handle) closePane(dataRoot, e.pane, cli, bridgeDir); throw e; }`; :205 `for (const sig of FORWARDED_SIGNALS) process.on(sig, forward);` runs only after the synchronous createPane.
findings.suggested_fix: Inside createPane, wrap everything after a handle is known in try/catch and rethrow with `{ pane: { handle } }` attached, so main() always closes it. Install the signal handlers before the CLI phase: on a signal before spawn, close the pane if one exists and exit 128+n.
findings.preconditions: orcad slow or failing between create and list, or the extension terminating a session during wrapper start-up.

votes.reasoning: claude-wrapper.mjs:151-152 calls runCli for 'terminal list' outside any try. runCli (118-124) uses execFileSync and JSON.parse, so a timeout (ETIMEDOUT), a non-zero exit, or output that is not JSON throws a raw error with no .pane property. The local 'pane' object holding the handle is lost. main() at 191-192 closes a pane only when e?.pane?.handle is set, so in this path the pane is never closed. Only the wrapper's own refuse() errors carry pane (lines 136 and 159). The 'create timed out after orcad already made the terminal' variant follows the same path, since execFileSync kills only the CLI client and has no handle to give back. That orcad finishes the create after the client is killed is runtime behaviour, but the list-failure path alone is enough to confirm the finding. The signal case is also correct: process.on(sig, forward) is installed only at line 205, after the synchronous createPane. A SIGTERM during the CLI phase takes the default action, kills the wrapper, and leaves a created pane in place. Installing the handlers earlier would not help either, because JS handlers cannot run while execFileSync blocks the loop. No guard elsewhere closes the pane. The impact is an orphan 'Claude Code' tab running cat: a user-visible correctness issue with no security effect.
votes.guard_or_evidence: theia/extensions/orca-agents/bin/claude-wrapper.mjs:151-158 (list call has no try and attaches no pane), :191-193 (close only when e.pane.handle exists), :205 (signal handlers installed after createPane)

findings.title: Claude start-up blocks on up to three synchronous 20 s Orca CLI calls before claude is spawned
findings.description: runCli uses execFileSync with CLI_TIMEOUT_MS = 20000. createPane can make three sequential calls (create, show, list) before claude is spawned, so a wedged but reachable orcad delays every Claude Code session by up to 60 s. During that time the event loop is blocked and nothing is forwarded. The orcad-data-root file is removed only when OrcaService stops orcad cleanly, so after a crash or hang the wrapper still trusts the stale file and pays the full timeouts on every session.
findings.scenario: orcad hangs: its process is alive and the socket accepts connections, but nothing answers. Every Claude Code chat the user opens waits about 40-60 s before claude starts, then runs unwrapped. The extension may report its own start-up timeout first.
findings.evidence: claude-wrapper.mjs:46 `const CLI_TIMEOUT_MS = 20000;` :119-121 `execFileSync(join(dataRoot, 'cli', 'bin', 'orca'), [...args, '--json'], { env, stdio: [...], timeout, encoding: 'utf8' })`; :134, :146, :152 three sequential calls.
findings.suggested_fix: Use one overall deadline for the pane phase (for example 3-5 s in total) instead of 20 s per call, or spawn claude at once and attach the pane identity only when it is ready within a short budget.
findings.preconditions: orcad alive but unresponsive while orcad-data-root still exists.

votes.reasoning: CLI_TIMEOUT_MS = 20000 (line 46), and runCli uses execFileSync (119-121). createPane can make three calls in sequence (134 create, 146 show, 152 list), all before spawn at 203, so the event loop is blocked for up to 60 s. Upstream's CLI client defaults to a 60 s request timeout (orca/src/cli/runtime/client.ts:80), so the wrapper's 20 s limit is the one that applies. orcad-data-root is removed only in OrcaService._stopTree (OrcaService.sys.mjs:630-633); the unexpected-exit/restart path (line 588) does not remove it. Two corrections to the claim: (a) the full 60 s needs create to succeed without a paneKey and then show and list to hang. A fully hung orcad times out at create, which costs about 20 s per session. (b) After a crash where the socket is gone, the CLI most likely fails fast with a connection error rather than paying the timeouts. The hang case stands as described. This is a latency correctness issue only.
votes.guard_or_evidence: claude-wrapper.mjs:46, :118-124, :134/:146/:152; OrcaService.sys.mjs:588 (restart does not remove the file) vs :630-633 (only clean stop removes it); orca/src/cli/runtime/client.ts:80 (CLI default 60 s)

findings.title: On Windows the backend still registers a POSIX sh launcher as the Claude Code process wrapper default
findings.description: TheiaService passes POWERBROWSER_ORCA_BRIDGE_DIR on win32 (bridgeDirFor returns a LOCALAPPDATA path), and onStart skips the POSIX mode checks there. It then writes the `#!/bin/sh` launcher with no extension and the frontend registers that path as the claudeCode.claudeProcessWrapper default. Windows cannot execute an extensionless sh script, so if the extension honours the default, Claude Code fails to start rather than running unwrapped. The wrapper is also inert on Windows even if it were reached, because readDataRoot requires `cli/bin/orca` while orcad writes `cli/bin/orca.exe` on win32. WINDOWS entry 53 tracks the missing Windows launcher, but the backend is not made inert on win32 meanwhile.
findings.scenario: A Windows build of PowerBrowser (deferred, but the code path exists) starts with a bridge folder. The frontend sets claudeCode.claudeProcessWrapper to %LOCALAPPDATA%\pb-orca-<hex>-bridge\claude-wrapper. Every Claude Code session then fails at spawn.
findings.evidence: claude-wrapper-launcher.ts:21 `return `#!/bin/sh\nexec ${shQuote(nodePath)} ...`;` orca-agents-backend-module.ts:40-48 (win32 skips the mode check and still calls writeLauncher); orca-agents-frontend-module.ts:33 registerOverride with that path; claude-wrapper.mjs:90 `existsSync(join(dataRoot, 'cli', 'bin', 'orca'))` against upstream orcad-cli-launcher.ts:72 `join(binDir, 'orca.exe')`.
findings.suggested_fix: Return undefined from getClaudeWrapperPath on win32 until a Windows launcher exists (for example an .exe shim), so the extension's own spawn stays untouched there.
findings.preconditions: A Windows build; the Claude Code extension honours the default-scope override (research assumption A5).

votes.reasoning: The code path exists as described. TheiaService._orcaBridgeDir (TheiaService.sys.mjs:792) calls OrcaEnv.bridgeDirFor with the node platform, which returns a LOCALAPPDATA path on win32 (OrcaEnv.sys.mjs:297-303), and passes it as POWERBROWSER_ORCA_BRIDGE_DIR (line 911). The backend onStart skips the uid/mode check only when POSIX (orca-agents-backend-module.ts:41) and still calls writeLauncher (48). writeLauncher always writes '#!/bin/sh' text with no extension (claude-wrapper-launcher.ts:21, 26). The frontend registers that path as the claudeCode.claudeProcessWrapper default (orca-agents-frontend-module.ts:33). readDataRoot requires cli/bin/orca (claude-wrapper.mjs:90), while upstream writes orca.exe on Windows (orcad-cli-launcher.ts:72), so the wrapper would be inert even if reached. The step that cannot be settled statically is whether the Claude Code extension honours the default-scope override (research assumption A5) and how its spawn on Windows treats an extensionless sh file: a hard spawn failure or something else. WINDOWS.md entry 53 is open for the missing Windows launcher, and D-40 ships v1.7 Linux-only, so no shipped build reaches this path. That owner deferral does not refute the observation that the backend is not made inert on win32.
votes.guard_or_evidence: orca-agents-backend-module.ts:40-48; claude-wrapper-launcher.ts:21; orca-agents-frontend-module.ts:33; TheiaService.sys.mjs:792,911; .planning/WINDOWS.md:70 (entry 53 open, D-40 Linux only)

findings.title: Pre-installed uBlock Origin never updates itself; it stays at the shipped version until a PowerBrowser release bumps the pin
findings.description: The XPI is pinned by AMO URL and SHA-256. stage-bundled-xpi.sh fetches it over HTTPS, checks the hash on every staging, deletes the file and fails on a mismatch, and copies it unmodified into distribution/extensions/. There is no ExtensionSettings policy, so the user can remove it, and Gecko's extensions.installedDistroAddon pref keeps a removed copy removed. A newer XPI in a later PowerBrowser release upgrades an existing copy when the app version changes. The branding prefs set extensions.update.autoUpdateDefault=false, so the AMO background check finds updates but never installs them. A security fix in uBlock Origin (a privileged add-on with access to all pages) reaches users only through a PowerBrowser release or a manual update.
findings.scenario: uBlock Origin 1.76.x has a vulnerability fixed in 1.76.1 on AMO. PowerBrowser users keep 1.76.0 until the bundled-xpi.json pin is bumped and released, or until they update it manually from the add-ons page.
findings.evidence: bundled-xpi.json:5-7 version/url/sha256 pin; stage-bundled-xpi.sh:25-34 hash check with delete and fail; powerbrowser/branding/release/pref/firefox-branding.js:176 `pref("extensions.update.autoUpdateDefault", false);` endpoint-allowlist.json:203 notes the found update does not install itself; upstream XPIInstall.sys.mjs:4336-4360 upgrade-on-app-change and removal-sticks logic.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the uBlock Origin pin part of the weekly re-pin job, or set a per-add-on auto-update override for the distribution add-on, so security updates do not depend on a full release.
findings.preconditions: An upstream uBlock Origin security release.

votes.reasoning: bundled-xpi.json:5-7 pins version 1.76.0, the AMO URL and the sha256. stage-bundled-xpi.sh:24-35 re-downloads when the hash differs, then checks again, deletes the file and fails on a mismatch, and copies the file unmodified. policies.json has an empty ExtensionSettings, and bundled-xpi.json's $comment documents the deliberate absence of force/normal_installed and that a removal sticks. firefox-branding.js:176 sets extensions.update.autoUpdateDefault=false, and endpoint-allowlist.json:203 records that the periodic check runs but the found update does not install itself. An AMO-signed uBlock Origin therefore stays at the shipped version until a PowerBrowser release bumps the pin or the user updates it by hand. This is an accepted design trade-off, not a vulnerability, and info is correct.
votes.guard_or_evidence: powerbrowser/packaging/bundled-xpi.json:5-7; powerbrowser/packaging/stage-bundled-xpi.sh:24-35; powerbrowser/branding/release/pref/firefox-branding.js:176; powerbrowser/endpoint-allowlist.json:203

findings.title: Agent hooks are upstream orcad's: it rewrites the user's real ~/.claude/settings.json and ~/.orca/agent-hooks, and the hook endpoint token is shared by every pane
findings.description: PowerBrowser registers no hook of its own, and the wrapper writes no settings, hooks or credentials. It only sets ORCA_PANE_KEY, ORCA_TAB_ID, ORCA_WORKTREE_ID and ORCA_AGENT_HOOK_ENDPOINT=<dataRoot>/agent-hooks/endpoint.env, and it strips every inherited ORCA_* name. The hooks come from upstream orcad: startOrcadManagedAgentHooks reconciles managed hooks into the real HOME, because HOME is on ORCAD_ENV_ALLOWLIST. The hook command runs "$HOME/.orca/agent-hooks/claude-hook.sh", which `.`-sources the file ORCA_AGENT_HOOK_ENDPOINT names. Two consequences follow. (1) Running PowerBrowser edits the user's ~/.claude/settings.json and the ~/.orca/agent-hooks scripts that an installed Orca desktop also manages; a version skew between the two is handled only by upstream's owner and lock logic. (2) endpoint.env holds one port and token for all panes. claude, and every tool process it runs (skip-permissions on, D-12), can read it and post status for any paneKey, so a prompt-injected agent can spoof other panes' status. Hook payloads are parsed by upstream's server, not by PowerBrowser code.
findings.scenario: A prompt-injected Claude session runs `. $ORCA_AGENT_HOOK_ENDPOINT` and posts a 'done' or 'waiting' event for another agent's paneKey, so Orca shows a false status for that pane. Separately, a user with Orca desktop installed finds ~/.claude/settings.json hook entries rewritten by PowerBrowser's orcad.
findings.evidence: claude-wrapper.mjs:95-104 claudeEnv; orca/src/main/orcad/orcad-managed-agent-hooks.ts reconcileStartupManagedAgentHooks; orca/src/main/agent-hooks/runtime-home-hook-command.ts:25 `"${HOME-}/.orca/agent-hooks/${scriptBaseName}.sh"`; orca/src/main/cursor/hook-script.ts:77-78 `. "$ORCA_AGENT_HOOK_ENDPOINT"`; OrcaEnv.sys.mjs:37-39 HOME allowlisted.
findings.suggested_fix: Record in INTERNAL-APIS.md or DECISIONS.md that PowerBrowser's orcad manages the user's real agent hook configuration. If panes must not spoof each other, upstream would need per-pane hook tokens.
findings.preconditions: Agent status hooks enabled (the default); an agent that reads text an attacker controls.

votes.reasoning: The wrapper only strips ORCA_* names and sets ORCA_PANE_KEY, ORCA_TAB_ID, ORCA_WORKTREE_ID and ORCA_AGENT_HOOK_ENDPOINT=<dataRoot>/agent-hooks/endpoint.env (claude-wrapper.mjs:95-104). It writes no hooks or settings. HOME is on ORCAD_ENV_ALLOWLIST (OrcaEnv.sys.mjs, allowlist block near line 37). Upstream orcad runs reconcileStartupManagedAgentHooks (orcad-managed-agent-hooks.ts:60). Upstream writes Claude settings at join(homedir(), configDirName, 'settings.json') (main/claude/hook-settings.ts:54) and hook scripts at ~/.orca/agent-hooks (installer-utils.ts:114). The hook command sources $ORCA_AGENT_HOOK_ENDPOINT (cursor/hook-script.ts:77-78). The endpoint file holds one port and token per server (server-runtime-env.ts:45-52), not one per pane. The agent-process capture is client-supplied (hook-process-capture.ts), so a same-uid process can forge it. The spoofing precondition is code running as the user inside an agent with skip-permissions. That is already more capability than the gain: such a process can also edit ~/.claude/settings.json or signal other panes directly. So the finding is an accurate observation of upstream behaviour and not a boundary crossing. Info is correct.
votes.guard_or_evidence: claude-wrapper.mjs:95-104; OrcaEnv.sys.mjs ORCAD_ENV_ALLOWLIST includes HOME; orca/src/main/orcad/orcad-managed-agent-hooks.ts:60; orca/src/main/claude/hook-settings.ts:54; orca/src/main/agent-hooks/installer-utils.ts:114; orca/src/main/agent-hooks/server/server-runtime-env.ts:45-52; orca/src/main/cursor/hook-script.ts:77-78

findings.title: Orca build jobs in the Release run can replace the release-linux artifact that sign-publish signs, because that artifact has no digest tied to the job that produced it
findings.description: v1.7 adds three hosted jobs to release.yml (windows-orca, macos-orca-arm64, macos-orca-x64) that run the pinned upstream Orca build: pnpm run rebuild:node, build:orcad, build:web, Orca's config/scripts, mobile generators and Vite. They run in the same workflow run as sign-publish. sign-publish downloads `release-linux` by name, checks only that the manifest's release_key matches the tree, then signs the MAR with the MAR key and publishes it to the update channel. build-linux exports no digest of release-linux; it outputs only `build`. Code in a hosted job runs as the runner user. It can rewrite the on-disk copy of a later action in its own job (actions/upload-artifact, already downloaded under _work/_actions at job set-up) and so obtain ACTIONS_RUNTIME_TOKEN. That token can delete and upload artifacts of the run. The windows-sidecar job uses a SHA256SUMS digest passed as a job output to defend against exactly this, but the Linux artifact has no such binding. The 'Linux ships alone' ruling and the comment 'a failure here never reaches a Linux job' cover failures only. A Windows or macOS Orca job can still change the Linux bytes silently. The exposure existed before v1.7 through windows-sidecar's Theia build. v1.7 adds three more jobs that build an upstream which moves every week (D-26).
findings.scenario: A compromised Orca tag, or a compromised npm package in Orca's lockfile at that tag, reaches main through the weekly re-pin. On the next Release dispatch, build code running in windows-orca patches _actions/actions/upload-artifact/<sha>/dist/upload/index.js. When that step runs, the patched code takes ACTIONS_RUNTIME_TOKEN and sends it out, or waits with it. After build-linux uploads release-linux, the attacker uses the token to delete it and upload a tarball, MAR and manifest of their own with the correct release_key. The owner approves the release environment, and sign-publish signs and publishes the attacker's MAR. Every installed client then applies it as a valid signed update.
findings.evidence: release.yml:1138-1142 `- name: Download the release artifacts (untrusted data, copied and signed, never executed)\n uses: actions/download-artifact@... with: name: release-linux` followed by release.yml:1151-1152 (only `jq -r .release_key` is compared) and release.yml:1205 `Sign the complete MAR`. Producer side: release.yml:217-228 uploads release-linux with no digest output (build-linux outputs only `build: ${{ steps.key_gate.outputs.build }}`, line 78). Untrusted code in the same run: release.yml:449-455 (windows-orca `bash scripts/fetch-orca.sh; bash scripts/build-orca.sh`), 2148-2153 and 2263-2268 (macOS). Contrast the windows-sidecar pattern: `sums_sha256` output plus `check-win-sidecar.sh check` (release.yml:353, 910).
findings.suggested_fix: Bind release-linux to build-linux the same way the hosted sidecar is bound: have build-linux write SHA256SUMS over the uploaded files and export its sha256 as a job output. sign-publish then runs check-win-sidecar.sh check (or an equivalent) on the downloaded directory before any signing step. Better still, move the Orca and sidecar builds into a separate workflow run whose artifacts sign-publish fetches only by run id and verified digest, so no code that runs upstream builds shares a run with the MAR-signing job.
findings.preconditions: Malicious code in the pinned Orca tag or its locked dependencies (actor f), merged by the weekly re-pin. The ACTIONS_RUNTIME_TOKEN has to stay usable until build-linux has uploaded, either because the attacker's job is still running then or because the token works after its job ends.

votes.reasoning:
Most of the cited code is as described. sign-publish (release.yml:1087-1092, needs only build-linux) downloads `release-linux` by name (1138-1142). It checks the manifest release_key against the tree (1151-1152), the manifest update_channel and the MAR channel (1184-1203), then signs (1205-1220). It assembles assets straight from release/ (1242-1259), and the attestation at 1261 covers whatever was downloaded. build-linux exports only `build` (78) and uploads release-linux with no digest output (217-228). windows-orca (376-491) and the macOS Orca jobs have no needs edge and run the same scripts/build-orca.sh in the same run. By contrast, windows-orca's own output is bound by sums_sha256 (382, 472-480). So the finding is right that no digest ties release-linux to build-linux.

The headline scenario fails test (4): its precondition already gives the attacker the capability. The same pinned Orca tag and lockfile are built inside build-linux itself (release.yml:169-174). That build runs `nix develop .#orca --command bash scripts/build-orca.sh` on legion as the runner user, in the workspace that is later packaged and uploaded. build-orca.sh:194-223 runs pnpm install, build-workspace-packages, rebuild:node, the mobile generators, build:mobile-web, build:orcad and build:web. Malicious code in Orca's source, or in any dependency that runs or bundles on Linux, can therefore change the Linux tarball and MAR directly before the upload at 217. It can also ship itself, because package-linux.sh:23-33 and 73 put out/orcad and out/web into the Linux package. A compromised Orca tag already reaches every Linux client as signed code, with no token theft and no artifact swap. The same applies to windows-sidecar's Theia build (it uses the same theia lockfile as build-linux:164). The workflow header (lines 6-9) states the design: release-linux is untrusted data, and the protection is the owner's approval of the release environment, not where the bytes came from.

What remains is narrower. A dependency that is installed or run only on win32 or darwin would run in windows-orca or the macOS Orca jobs and never in build-linux. Examples are a platform-gated optional binary such as a win32 rollup, esbuild or lightningcss binary that Vite calls during the build. For that actor the cross-job path is real, and the 'Linux ships alone' comments (264, 375) cover only failures, not tampering. It still depends on runtime behaviour I cannot settle statically: whether the ACTIONS_RUNTIME_TOKEN taken in windows-orca can still delete and re-upload the run artifact `release-linux` after build-linux uploads it. windows-orca has a 90-minute timeout (378). build-linux runs a Gecko build of roughly 50 minutes plus the Theia, Orca and container steps, with a 240-minute timeout (74). The attacker therefore needs the token to stay valid after its own job ends, or the timings to overlap. Whether a run-scoped artifact token can delete an artifact another job created is also runtime behaviour.

Severity is medium, not high. The general precondition is equivalent to the gain, so this is a defence-in-depth gap: build-linux exports no release-linux digest for sign-publish to check, the way sums_sha256 is checked for Windows. It matters only for a platform-gated dependency compromise and only with an unconfirmed token lifetime.

Confirming evidence: release.yml:78 (only `build` is exported), 1138-1152 (download by name, release_key check only), 376-382 (windows-orca has no needs edge, same run)

findings.title: Pinned Orca build code runs unsandboxed on the persistent self-hosted runner legion, outside the release container
findings.description: build-linux runs on legion, a non-ephemeral self-hosted runner (user pb-runner, work dir /var/lib/pb-runner, kept between jobs). The Gecko build runs inside a rootless podman container that is rebuilt every release from a digest-pinned base. The new Orca step instead runs `nix develop .#orca --command bash scripts/build-orca.sh` directly on the host, and that executes Orca's own build scripts. The orca-packaged-tree row then imports orca/src/shared/*.ts on the host (scripts/lib/orca-artifacts.mjs importTs), which also executes Orca code. build-windows on legion fetches Orca and imports the same TypeScript inside the container. The Orca pin advances weekly through bot PRs with auto-merge armed (D-26). Code running as pb-runner persists between jobs and can read the runner's registration credentials in its state directory. It can therefore tamper with every later build-linux output. sign-publish treats that output as data and signs it without checking its content, and sign-windows signs what legion stages. Compromise of legion is therefore equal to compromise of the Linux update channel, and the docs already state it is equal to the Windows signing identity. Threat T-68-SC states that Orca's build runs 'only in the read-only job'. That holds inside the release train but not in release.yml.
findings.scenario: A malicious Orca release, such as a typosquatted dependency added to Orca's pnpm-lock.yaml, is re-pinned and merged. The next release dispatch runs build-orca.sh on legion as pb-runner. The build code installs a persistent hook (for example a modified file under /var/lib/pb-runner, or by taking the runner's .credentials and registering an impostor). Every later release then gets a backdoored tarball or MAR that sign-publish signs and ships to all installed clients.
findings.evidence: release.yml:169-174 `- name: Build Orca from source at the pin (orcad, web client) ... bash scripts/fetch-orca.sh\n nix develop .#orca --command bash scripts/build-orca.sh` (host shell), versus release.yml:176-188 where the Gecko build runs in `podman run --rm ... pb-gecko-build`. build-orca.sh:194-223 runs `pnpm run rebuild:node`, `node config/scripts/build-workspace-packages.mjs`, `node mobile/scripts/*.mjs`, `pnpm run build:mobile-web/build:orcad/build:web`. release.yml:212 adds row `orca-packaged-tree`, whose verify-orca-packaged-tree.mjs:211 calls orcaArtifactTables(join(REPO_ROOT,'orca')), and orca-artifacts.mjs:55 `return await import(pathToFileURL(file).href);`. docs/RELEASING.md:47 and 342-346 describe legion as non-ephemeral.
findings.suggested_fix: Build Orca for Linux on a GitHub-hosted runner, as windows-orca and the macOS jobs already do, and pass it to build-linux as data admitted by a SHA256SUMS digest output. Alternatively, run build-orca.sh and the orca-packaged-tree import inside the rootless podman container that is rebuilt from the pinned base, with no network after install. Replace the TypeScript import in orca-artifacts.mjs with a parse that does not execute the module, at least wherever it runs on legion.
findings.preconditions: Compromised upstream Orca tag or locked dependency (actor f), merged through the weekly re-pin PR with the owner's approval.

votes.reasoning:
I traced the code path and it holds. release.yml:169-174 runs `bash scripts/fetch-orca.sh` and then `nix develop .#orca --command bash scripts/build-orca.sh` in the host shell of the build-linux job on legion. Only the Gecko build (release.yml:183-188) and packaging (:199-202) run in `podman run --rm ... pb-gecko-build`. `nix develop` only sets up the environment and does not isolate anything.

build-orca.sh uses `--ignore-scripts` for both installs (:194, :202), so lifecycle scripts are off. It still executes Orca-controlled code and locked-dependency code on the host:
- `node config/scripts/build-workspace-packages.mjs` (:195)
- `pnpm run rebuild:node` (:196), which is a native rebuild
- three `node mobile/scripts/*.mjs` generators (:206-208)
- `pnpm run build:mobile-web`, `build:orcad` and `build:web` (:209-223), which run Orca's package.json scripts and bundler configs

The orca-packaged-tree row (release.yml:212, registered at verify-platform.sh:6788) also runs on the host. It calls `orcaArtifactTables(join(REPO_ROOT,'orca'))` (verify-orca-packaged-tree.mjs:211), and `importTs` does a dynamic `import()` of `orca/src/shared/*.ts` (orca-artifacts.mjs:55), which executes that module's top level.

What reaches this path:
- The pin advances through bot PRs with auto-merge armed (release-train.yml:1059, :1147; D-26).
- The owner's approving review and main-review are the only gates.
- The header of rebase-orca.yml says "This is the only job that runs Orca's code". The `T-68-SC` rows (68-02-PLAN.md:304) say "only in the read-only job". Both are contradicted by release.yml.
- docs/RELEASING.md:342-346 and :1968-1969 confirm legion is non-ephemeral and keeps /var/lib/pb-runner between jobs.
- The pre-job hook (RELEASING.md:381-388) refuses only run shape (ref, event, BASH_ENV and similar). It does not sandbox anything.
- The registration-token file and the MAR key store are stated to be unreadable by pb-runner (RELEASING.md:376-379, :1146). That limits credential exposure but does not block host execution.

Two runtime steps I cannot settle statically:
- whether the runner's own `.credentials` and `.credentials_rsaparams` in its state directory are readable by job processes (this is standard for a same-uid NixOS github-runner);
- which persistence location survives `actions/checkout`'s clean.

Why medium and not high: the precondition is a malicious Orca release or locked dependency merged with the owner's approval. That compromise already backdoors the shipped product on its own, because orcad and the web client built from that code ship in the tarball that sign-publish signs, so a container would not prevent it. What host execution adds is persistence on legion across later releases (after the bad pin is reverted), possible theft of the runner registration credentials, and tampering with what legion stages for sign-windows.

The weakness is not new in kind. Theia's `yarn build` and the `node-gyp rebuild` of drivelist already run on the same host (release.yml:164-166). Orca makes it worse, because a dependency graph that changes weekly now runs on the persistent host. This is a defence-in-depth gap with a concrete path, plus a threat-model statement that is false for release.yml. It is not a boundary an outside attacker can cross without first compromising upstream and getting the owner to merge.
votes.guard_or_evidence: .github/workflows/release.yml:169-174 (host-shell build-orca.sh, outside the podman container at :183-188); scripts/build-orca.sh:195-223 (Orca build code executed); scripts/lib/orca-artifacts.mjs:55 via scripts/verify-orca-packaged-tree.mjs:211 and release.yml:212 (host import of Orca TS); docs/RELEASING.md:342-346,1968-1969 (non-ephemeral runner); release-train.yml:1059,1147 (auto-merge armed, owner review is the gate); contradicts rebase-orca.yml header and 68-02-PLAN.md:304 T-68-SC

findings.title: The green re-pin replay that auto-merge relies on is reported by the upstream code it is meant to check
findings.description: bump-pr-orca arms `gh pr merge --auto` when rebase-orca reports stage `replayed`. That stage is decided in the job that installs and runs the new Orca tag. The typecheck:web and typecheck:node commands are scripts from Orca's own package.json. tsc, Vite and every build tool come from Orca's lockfile at the new tag. During the replay step, Orca code can also write $GITHUB_ENV (for example BASH_ENV) or edit the workspace to steer the later 'Name the stage' and 'notices' steps. The PR's required `verify` check builds nothing (verify.yml), and no other workflow builds Orca, so nothing outside the job under test runs the new code. The only remaining gate is the owner's approving review (main-review), and the diff it shows is a pin hash and regenerated seam context. A review of that diff cannot see what changed upstream. T-68-12 ('vacuous green replay') covers SKIP lines but not a green result forged by hostile upstream code.
findings.scenario: An Orca tag whose package.json sets `"typecheck:web": "exit 0"`, or whose build does harmful work and still exits 0, makes rebase-orca report `replayed` with notices `unchanged`. bump-pr-orca publishes chore/orca-<tag> with auto-merge armed and a body that states the typecheck, rows, orcad and brand scan all passed. Once the owner approves, it merges, and the next release builds the tag (see the legion and artifact findings).
findings.evidence: release-train.yml:1061 `if: ${{ !inputs.dry-run && needs.rebase-orca.outputs.stage == 'replayed' }}`; release-train.yml:1176 `gh pr merge "$PR" --auto --merge`; rebase-orca.yml:112-120 `if [ "$OUTCOME" = "success" ]; then echo "stage=replayed"`; rebase-orca.sh:177 `capture eval 'cd "$root/orca" && "$run" "$script"'` (Orca's own scripts); rebase-orca.sh:289-291 `corepack pnpm ... run "$1"`. verify.yml has no Orca build (only rebase-orca.yml, release-train.yml and release.yml reference orca).
findings.suggested_fix: Treat `replayed` as a compatibility signal, not a security signal, and say so in the PR body. Do not arm auto-merge for an upstream code change. Show the owner the upstream compare link and commit range from the old pin to the new one in the PR body. Optionally require a second signal computed outside the job that runs the code (for example a check that Orca's lockfile adds no new packages, run in bump-pr-orca over git data only), and arm auto-merge only when the lockfile is unchanged.
findings.preconditions: Compromised upstream Orca tag (actor f).

votes.reasoning: The cited path exists. rebase-orca.yml:118-120 writes stage=replayed whenever the replay step's outcome is success. That step (rebase-orca.yml:104-106) runs Orca's own package scripts through rebase-orca.sh:177 and orca_pnpm_run (rebase-orca.sh:289-291), so the code under test decides its own exit status. It also inherits GITHUB_ENV/GITHUB_OUTPUT. bump-pr-orca (release-train.yml:1062) gates on that stage, and release-train.yml:1176 arms auto-merge when notices is unchanged. verify.yml builds Theia only (lines 67-93) and nothing else builds Orca before merge. The finding overstates the impact, though. The forged green buys nothing that a hostile tag which simply typechecks and builds would not get anyway. Typecheck:web/node are correctness gates, not checks against hostile upstream code. bump-pr-orca rebuilds the PR tree itself with --replay-only from tracked data (release-train.yml:1092-1099), so the only extra bytes the compromised job can inject are the notices artifact. When that artifact is carried, auto-merge is withheld (1166-1177). Forging notices=unchanged only drops Orca's notices update. The real gate is the owner's approving review in .github/settings/ruleset-main-review.json (required_approving_review_count 1, dismiss_stale_reviews_on_push). D-26 explicitly accepts an automated weekly re-pin, which keeps the verdict but frames the risk as accepted. The genuine residue: the PR body asserts checks passed when the checked code produced that result, and a pin-hash diff cannot show what changed upstream. That is inherent to pinning an upstream and is low severity.
votes.guard_or_evidence: rebase-orca.yml:118-120; rebase-orca.sh:177,289-291; release-train.yml:1062,1092-1099,1163,1173-1177; .github/settings/ruleset-main-review.json (1 approving review required, verify the only required status check); DECISIONS.md D-26 accepts automated re-pin

findings.title: rebase-orca runs untrusted Orca code in the same release-train run as renovate-licensing-publish, so it can replace the notices artifact the bot commits
findings.description: Plan 51-09 split the Theia licensing regeneration so that no untrusted code shares a context with what the bot publishes. renovate-licensing-publish (bot environment, App token) downloads `renovate-licensing-notices` by name from the current run and commits it to chore/theia-theia. rebase-orca now runs in the same run whenever the Theia tick and the Orca tick fall on the same sweep, or when the owner dispatches with both flags. It executes Orca's install and build with a later actions/upload-artifact step on disk, so the Orca code can obtain ACTIONS_RUNTIME_TOKEN and delete and re-upload any artifact in the run. The same applies to `release-train-maintenance-state`, which the next sweep downloads (prev-run-id) to decide which maintenance rows count as newly red.
findings.scenario: On a sweep that is both the first after the month's last Thursday and the first of an ISO week, the hostile Orca build takes the runtime token. Once renovate-licensing uploads, it replaces renovate-licensing-notices with a LICENSING.md and THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt of its own. The listing check `ls -A == 'LICENSING.md THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt'` passes, and the bot commits the forged notices to the Theia PR. Alternatively, it uploads a release-train-maintenance-state that marks red rows as already red, which suppresses the transition comment for a watchdog failure.
findings.evidence: release-train.yml:1046-1055 `rebase-orca: ... uses: ./.github/workflows/rebase-orca.yml` (same run); rebase-orca.yml:138 `uses: actions/upload-artifact@...` after the untrusted step at rebase-orca.yml:104-106; release-train.yml:931-936 `Download the regenerated notices ... name: renovate-licensing-notices` with the comment 'This run's artifact only'; release-train.yml:947 checks only the file names; release-train.yml:1944-1946 uploads release-train-maintenance-state, which the next run reads at 1881-1886.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass each notices artifact's sha256 as a job output of the producing job (renovate-licensing outputs.head already exists, so add outputs.notices-sha256) and verify it in renovate-licensing-publish before committing. Do the same for maintenance-state. Or run the Orca re-pin as its own workflow (rebase-orca.yml dispatched separately) so no upstream code shares a run with bot-environment consumers.
findings.preconditions: Compromised upstream Orca tag (actor f), and a run that includes both the Orca re-pin and the Theia inflow or maintenance sweep.

votes.reasoning: The co-scheduling is real. detect-orca (release-train.yml:1004-1006) and renovate-theia (758-760) both hang off sweep-clock, with orca-due and theia-due computed independently in one sweep (722-750), or set together by owner dispatch flags. rebase-orca is a reusable-workflow job in the same run (1046-1055) with a 90-minute timeout, running Orca's install, build and typecheck on a hosted runner. renovate-licensing-publish downloads `renovate-licensing-notices` by name from the current run (931-936). Its only content check is the file-name listing at 947. It then copies the files into target/ and commits them under the bot identity (960-970) with the App token minted afterwards (973-993). Nothing compares the artifact content with what renovate-licensing produced (for example a digest passed as a job output). The step I cannot settle statically: whether code in a run step of the rebase job can obtain a usable ACTIONS_RUNTIME_TOKEN and use it to delete and re-create an artifact another job in the same run uploaded, before renovate-licensing-publish downloads it. Two routes exist: reading the Runner.Worker process memory or environ (passwordless sudo on hosted runners), or a later node action step in the same job (the upload-artifact at rebase-orca.yml:138 runs only when notices changed). Cross-job deletion inside a run is what upload-artifact's overwrite and merge/delete-merged rely on, so the mechanism is credible. The race window depends on runtime timing. The maintenance-state half is weaker. The report job, which needs rebase-orca (1628), uploads release-train-maintenance-state with overwrite:true (1944-1954) after the rebase job has ended. Tampering with it therefore needs the exfiltrated token to stay valid after its job completes, a second runtime step. Impact is bounded: the forged notices land on chore/theia-theia, where Renovate automerge is off and the owner merges (comment at 756). The suppressed transition comment still leaves the issue body patched red (1922-1929). Medium as a defence-in-depth gap against the plan 51-09 separation stands.
votes.guard_or_evidence: release-train.yml:722-750 (independent theia/orca ticks), 1046-1055 (same run), 931-936 and 947 (name-only check), 960-970 (bot commit of artifact bytes); rebase-orca.yml:73-76 (contents: read does not scope the runtime token), 104-106, 138; release-train.yml:1628 and 1944-1954 (state upload after rebase-orca ends)

findings.title: sign-windows signs Orca PE files from the legion zip after matching names only, although the admitted SHA256SUMS carries a digest for each file
findings.description: sign-windows admits windows-orca/SHA256SUMS against the hosted job's digest output. orcaChecks then compares the PE files under orca/ in the legion-built zip with the SHA256SUMS entries by path only. The per-file sha256 values in the admitted manifest are parsed and thrown away, and the staged bytes are never hashed against them. legion (persistent, and now running Orca's Linux build) can therefore swap the content of any Orca PE file and have it Authenticode-signed under the project identity. Signing is currently skipped (no Azure account, R14), so this is latent.
findings.scenario: Once Azure signing is configured, a compromised legion replaces orca/out/orcad/node_modules/node-pty/build/Release/pty.node in the staged Windows zip with a malicious DLL of the same name. sign-windows lists the file as required, finds it present and signs it.
findings.evidence: win-sign-list.mjs:155-158 `const m = /^[0-9a-f]{64} [ *](.+)$/.exec(line); ... listed.push(m[1]);` (the digest is dropped); 161-167 compare name sets only; release.yml:910-912 `check-win-sidecar.sh check windows-orca "$PB_WIN_ORCA_SUMS_SHA256"` then `win-sign-list.mjs --list ... --orca-sums windows-orca/SHA256SUMS`.
findings.suggested_fix: In orcaChecks, keep the digest from each SHA256SUMS line and require sha256(<pkg>/orca/<path>) to equal it for every staged orca/ file, PE or not. Fail before signing on any mismatch.
findings.preconditions: Azure signing configured, and a compromised legion runner.

votes.reasoning: The code does what the finding says. win-sign-list.mjs:155 matches `^[0-9a-f]{64} [ *](.+)$` and pushes only m[1] (158), dropping the digest. orcaChecks compares name sets only (160-167). Nothing in sign-windows hashes staged orca/ files against windows-orca/SHA256SUMS: release.yml:910-912 admits the SUMS file by its digest, then calls win-sign-list. The staged bytes come from legion's release-windows zip (release.yml ~800-847), and jsign signs them (~940-942). The precondition, a compromised legion with Azure signing configured, already gives the same capability without this gap. The Gecko PE files (xul.dll, the main .exe and the rest) are also built on legion and signed after a name-only manifest comparison (listChecks 184-189). A compromised legion can therefore get arbitrary bytes Authenticode-signed today by replacing xul.dll. The Orca digest gap removes a hosted-build integrity property Phase 68 intended for orca/, but it grants no new capability to this attacker. Signing is also skipped under R14 (release.yml azure_config step). The script header's claim that 'legion's output never decides which bytes get the Authenticode signature' is inaccurate for both halves. Real defect, information severity.
votes.guard_or_evidence: scripts/win-sign-list.mjs:155-167 (digest discarded), 184-189 (Gecko PE files also name-only); release.yml:910-912; release.yml azure_config step (signing=false when AZURE_CLIENT_ID unset, R14)

findings.title: Upstream build output can write the text of the Orca stop issue
findings.description: The stage output is the first log line that starts with 'rebase-orca: FAIL -- '. The log includes everything Orca's build, typecheck and probes print, because capture() echoes their output. A hostile upstream can print such a line with any text and then exit non-zero. The report job writes that text into an issue created with the job token, in the repository's release-train label set. The text can carry @mentions, links and misleading 'Next step' instructions. It is a single line, so GITHUB_OUTPUT cannot be split.
findings.scenario: Orca's build prints 'rebase-orca: FAIL -- build: security regression, see https://evil.example/fix.sh and run curl ... | sh @owner' and exits 1. The tracking issue 'release-train: orca vX.Y.Z stopped' shows that text as the stage, next to the official run URL.
findings.evidence: rebase-orca.yml:122 `LINE=$(grep -m1 '^rebase-orca: FAIL -- ' "$RUNNER_TEMP/rebase.log" ...)`; rebase-orca.sh:73-74 `OUT="$("$@" 2>&1)" ... printf '%s\n' "$OUT"`; release-train.yml:1700 `printf '...Stage: \`%s\`...' "$TAG" "$STAGE"`.
findings.suggested_fix: Have rebase-orca.sh write its own stage line to a separate file descriptor or file that composed commands cannot write to, and read the stage from there. Restrict the published stage to the stage keyword plus a [A-Za-z0-9_./:@ -] detail of bounded length.
findings.preconditions: Compromised upstream Orca tag (actor f).

votes.reasoning: capture() (rebase-orca.sh:72-75) prints the full combined output of each captured command before the stage's own red line (64), and the workflow tees stdout and stderr to rebase.log (rebase-orca.yml:106). stage_typecheck runs Orca's own package script (rebase-orca.sh:177, orca_pnpm_run 289-291) through capture, so a hostile tag can print a column-0 line beginning 'rebase-orca: FAIL -- ' and exit non-zero. That line precedes PB's own red line, and grep -m1 at rebase-orca.yml:122 selects it as the stage output. The report job passes it through env (no expression injection) and printf %s into the issue body inside a single-backtick code span (release-train.yml:1700). It then creates or edits 'release-train: orca <tag> stopped' with the job token (1701-1707). The code span would neutralise links and mentions, but nothing strips backticks from STAGE. A line containing a backtick closes the span, so markdown links, @mentions and false 'Next step' text render in the issue next to the real run URL. A newline cannot be injected because grep returns a single line and GITHUB_OUTPUT is written with echo. The precondition (a compromised upstream tag) already includes code execution in a CI runner, so the incremental harm is a phishing-capable issue body. Low.
votes.guard_or_evidence: rebase-orca.sh:64,72-75,177; rebase-orca.yml:106,122-123; release-train.yml:1689-1707 (STAGE inserted into `%s` with no backtick sanitising)

findings.title: The release runner user is in libvirtd (root-equivalent on legion), and v1.7 runs Orca's whole from-source build on that persistent runner outside any container
findings.description: legion-pb.nix puts pb-runner, the user every release.yml job on legion runs as, into the libvirtd group. Read-write access to qemu:///system is root-equivalent: a domain can be defined with host filesystem passthrough or a host block device. The runner is non-ephemeral (ephemeral = false, line 37), and LIBVIRT_DEFAULT_URI=qemu:///system is exported to every job. v1.7 adds a build-linux step that runs `nix develop .#orca --command bash scripts/build-orca.sh` directly on the host, not inside the rootless pb-gecko-build container that Gecko is built in. build-orca.sh installs with --ignore-scripts, but it then runs upstream Orca code and code from the npm closure: config/scripts/*.mjs, vite and esbuild with their plugins, `pnpm run rebuild:node` (node-gyp), and mobile's generator scripts. All of that runs as pb-runner. The pre-job hook keeps out other repos, other workflows and fork PRs. It does nothing against code inside the pinned build inputs.
findings.scenario: Threat (f): an Orca re-pin (rebase-orca or the release-train repin-orca, weekly) takes in a compromised Orca commit, or a lockfile package whose build-time code is malicious (a vite plugin, or a package whose module top level runs when esbuild or vite loads it). On the next release dispatch the build-linux job runs that code as pb-runner on legion. It calls `virsh define` on a domain that mounts / from the host and boots it, which gives root on the owner's workstation. Because the runner is persistent, it can also leave files in /var/lib/pb-runner, .mozbuild/pnpm-store or the corepack cache that alter later release builds. The hosted signer then signs a tampered tarball.
findings.evidence: systemd/legion-pb.nix:37 `ephemeral = false;`, :48 `LIBVIRT_DEFAULT_URI = "qemu:///system";`, :55 `extraGroups = [ "libvirtd" ];`. .github/workflows/release.yml:73 `runs-on: [self-hosted, powerbrowser-release]`, :169-174 `bash scripts/fetch-orca.sh` / `nix develop .#orca --command bash scripts/build-orca.sh` (host shell, not podman), unlike :187 where Gecko is built in `podman run ... pb-gecko-build`. scripts/build-orca.sh:195-223 runs build-workspace-packages.mjs, rebuild:node, the mobile generators, build:mobile-web, build:orcad and build:web.
findings.suggested_fix: Run the libvirt Windows-matrix jobs as a separate runner user and registration, or switch them to qemu:///session, so the user that builds third-party code has no libvirt socket. Move the Orca build (and the Theia yarn build) into the rootless container the way the Gecko build already runs. Prefer just-in-time ephemeral runner registration so that one job cannot leave state for the next.
findings.preconditions: A malicious change reaches the pinned Orca commit or its lockfile closure (upstream compromise plus a merged re-pin), and the owner dispatches a release.

votes.reasoning:
I traced every cited step.

1. systemd/legion-pb.nix sets pb-runner as the runner user (:40), `ephemeral = false` (:37), `LIBVIRT_DEFAULT_URI = "qemu:///system"` (:48) and `extraGroups = [ "libvirtd" ]` (:55). It also enables libvirtd (:64).

2. The group grants full access. The NixOS libvirtd module on legion's channel sets `auth_unix_rw = "polkit"` (virtualisation/libvirtd.nix:16). Its polkit rule grants org.libvirt.unix.manage to `subject.isInGroup("libvirtd")` (:639). Management access to qemu:///system is root-equivalent: a domain can pass host paths or host block devices through to the guest.

3. The runner sandbox does not block this. github-runner/service.nix:278-315 sets PrivateUsers, ProtectSystem=strict and NoNewPrivileges, but RestrictAddressFamilies includes AF_UNIX. A read-only mount does not stop connect() on a socket. polkit takes the caller's uid and group membership from the host side, not from the job's user namespace. The file's own comment (:27-28) says socket reachability is unverified. The design intends virsh to work for win-matrix-run.sh, and the comment says to add serviceOverrides if it fails. So "it does not work" would be a bug the owner fixes, not a guard.

4. Orca's build runs on the host, outside the container. release.yml build-linux runs on [self-hosted, powerbrowser-release]. The step "Build Orca from source at the pin" runs `bash scripts/fetch-orca.sh` and then `nix develop .#orca --command bash scripts/build-orca.sh` in the runner's host shell, not inside podman. The Gecko build and the packaging steps do use `podman run ... pb-gecko-build`. scripts/build-orca.sh installs with `--ignore-scripts` (:194, :202) and then runs Orca and closure code as pb-runner: config/scripts/build-workspace-packages.mjs (:195), `pnpm run rebuild:node` (:196), the three mobile generators (:206-208), build:mobile-web, build:orcad and build:web (:209-223).

5. Both cited changes are new in v1.7, according to git history: the libvirtd group in fb9fbddc (59-02) and the build-orca step in 071d6f67 (68-01).

6. The pre-job hook and the main-only/dispatch-only checks filter which repo, workflow and event can run a job. They do nothing about code inside the pinned build inputs.

Why medium rather than high:

- The precondition is hard to arrange: an upstream Orca or npm-closure compromise must land in a re-pin, and the re-pin must merge. release-train.yml:1059/1147 arms auto-merge, but main-review and the owner's approving review remain the gate. Some PRs never get auto-merge at all (:1167-1176).
- The main harm in the scenario follows from the precondition alone, without libvirt. Code that runs in the release build as pb-runner can already tamper with the tarball and leave files in the persistent workDir and caches before the hosted signer signs. The libvirt group adds one thing: root on legion.
- The exposure is not limited to Orca. The Theia step (`yarn build` after `yarn install --ignore-scripts`) also runs npm-closure build code in the host shell as pb-runner. The real gap is libvirtd membership for the user that runs all host-shell build steps, not Orca specifically.

No owner decision in DECISIONS.md accepts this risk. D-26 automates weekly re-pins, which increases how often new closure code arrives.

So: CONFIRMED as a real pb-runner-to-root path with a concrete chain, rated as a defence-in-depth gap given the supply-chain precondition.
votes.guard_or_evidence: systemd/legion-pb.nix:55 (libvirtd group), :48 (qemu:///system); NixOS virtualisation/libvirtd.nix:16 + :639 (polkit grants manage to libvirtd group); github-runner/service.nix:305-310 (AF_UNIX allowed); .github/workflows/release.yml build-linux step "Build Orca from source at the pin" (host shell, not podman); scripts/build-orca.sh:195-223

findings.title: The endpoint allowlist does not cover several hosts Orca hosting contacts, and two 'allow' rows justified by other features silently admit Orca's requests
findings.description: The allowlist claims to be 'the single machine-readable source of truth for every endpoint this build is allowed to contact'. Two rows hide Orca traffic. www.google.com has disposition allow (unattended) with a Widevine-redirect reason, but Orca's side panel and settings fetch https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=<agent or repo host>. The v1.7 rows themselves say whether launching straight into Orca mode contacts these hosts is an open owner item. Because www.google.com is 'allow', an unattended favicon request to it passes the verdict model. Only the gstatic redirect targets are user-initiated. The same applies to cdn.jsdelivr.net (allow, reason: uBlock filter lists), which also admits Orca's web-client emoji image loads (cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/emoji-datasource-*). Hosts that the shipped Orca bundles contact on a user action and that have no row at all: huggingface.co (speech model download), storage.googleapis.com (skill install), nodejs.org and unofficial-builds.nodejs.org (orcad remote install), avatars.githubusercontent.com, app.orca.dev (skill share; not under .onorca.dev), linear.app or the Linear API, api.atlassian.com, api.bitbucket.org and dev.azure.com.
findings.scenario: PowerBrowser starts in Orca mode. The Orca sidebar loads its agent icons from www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=claude.ai&sz=64 before any click, which tells Google which agents the user has and, through repo-icon.ts, the hostnames of the user's repository websites. verify-endpoints passes, because www.google.com is an unattended 'allow' host for Widevine. Separately, a user who turns on speech input triggers a huggingface.co download that the allowlist marks as an unknown-host failure, so the gate's picture of v1.7 egress is incomplete in both directions.
findings.evidence: powerbrowser/endpoint-allowlist.json:211 `"host": "www.google.com", "disposition": "allow"` with reason `part of the same Widevine update-check flow`. The t0..t3.gstatic.com rows: `Whether launching straight into the Orca mode may contact it is an open owner item`. orca/src/renderer/src/lib/agent-catalog.tsx:105 and orca/src/shared/repo-icon.ts:28 build `https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=...`. orca/src/main/speech/model-download-catalog.ts builds huggingface.co URLs. orca/src/main/runtime/runtime-skill-install-commands.ts:84 uses `['https://storage.googleapis.com']`. orca/src/shared/node-runtime-pin.ts names nodejs.org and unofficial-builds.nodejs.org. orca/out/web contains cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/emoji-datasource-* image URLs.
findings.suggested_fix: Give Orca's favicon traffic its own handling. Either route the s2/favicons and emoji image loads through a local placeholder in the overlay, or make the verdict model attribute www.google.com by path or initiator so that an Orca-originated request needs a user action. Add user-initiated rows, with reasons tied to the Orca source, for every host the shipped Orca bundles can reach. Add a static check that extracts hosts from orca/out and compares them with the allowlist both ways.
findings.preconditions: Orca mode or its side panel is shown (favicons), or the user uses the named Orca features.

An 'allow' host passes whatever the initiator and whether or not the user acted. www.google.com is 'allow' with a Widevine-redirect reason only, and orca/src/renderer/src/lib/agent-catalog.tsx:105 and orca/src/shared/repo-icon.ts:28 load https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=..., which also appears in the shipped orca/out/web assets. Absent hosts fail rather than pass, so that half is incompleteness, not masking. findings.title: Driver has no SKIP verdict: a row that prints SKIP and exits 0 is recorded PASS, and --gate reports every check green
findings.description: The run loop decides a row only from the exit status of the row process and the leak leg. It has no SKIP state and does not read the row's output. Every v1.7 live row that guards a security requirement returns 0 after printing 'SKIP --' when one of its preconditions is missing, so the summary prints '<label>: PASS'. run_gate_mode only looks at '<label>: FAIL' lines, so --gate prints 'every registered check is green at this commit' while those rows asserted nothing. The project already treats this as a defect elsewhere: scripts/rebase-orca.sh makes any SKIP line red inside the replay, and WINDOWS 69 records that orca-agent-status-live was counted PASS on a SKIP in gate runs 4 and 5.
findings.scenario: A gate run on a host where theia/node_modules/typescript is missing, where orca/out/orcad/orcad.js was not rebuilt, or where the Claude sign-in expires in under 60 minutes. orca-credential-store-live (credential store) prints 'SKIP -- theia/node_modules/typescript is not installed' and exits 0. no-remote-agent-port-live (D-11) and orca-pairing-containment-live (pairing containment) print SKIP with no built orcad. orca-agent-status-live prints SKIP on the sign-in margin. orca-slotless-start, the permanent re-pin proof, prints SKIP on any host where installedOrcaPaths(orcaDir, homedir()) finds ~/.local/bin/orca-ide or /opt/Orca/orca-ide. Each row is summarised as PASS, and the gate exits 0 with 'PASS' or 'PASS-WITH-EXCLUSIONS'.
findings.evidence: scripts/verify-platform.sh:6975-6990: `setsid $cmd & ... wait "$CURRENT_CHECK_PID" || row_ok=0 ... if [ "$row_ok" -eq 1 ]; then SUMMARY+=("$label: PASS")`. Gate :7066-7067 `extract_failed_labels` greps only `': FAIL$'`, and :7199-7200 prints `--gate PASS -- ... every registered check is green`. Row exits: verify-orca-credential-store-live.mjs:120 `if (!ts) { console.log(`${NAME}: SKIP -- theia/node_modules/typescript is not installed`); return 0; }`; verify-no-remote-agent-port-live.mjs:286 `if (skip) { console.log(`${NAME}: SKIP -- ${skip}`); return 0; }`; verify-orca-pairing-containment.mjs:257 `if (pre.skip) {...; return 0; }`; verify-orca-agent-status-live.mjs:199-200 `const unseeded = seedClaudeLogin(); if (unseeded) return { skip: unseeded };`; verify-orca-slotless-start.mjs:130-131 (installedOrcaPaths default home = os.homedir(), lib/orca-run.mjs:276). Contrast: scripts/rebase-orca.sh:25 `SKIP is red inside the replay`.
findings.suggested_fix: Give the driver a SKIP verdict. Have rows exit with a distinct code (for example 3) or print a fixed last line, record '<label>: SKIP', and make --gate fail on any SKIP that is not keyed to an open ledger entry, the same way FAIL exclusions are keyed. Under --gate, turn a missing typescript, a missing orcad build or an installed Orca into a FAIL.

votes.reasoning:
I traced the full path. In run_own_checks (scripts/verify-platform.sh:6974-6991), a bash or node row gets PASS or FAIL from two things only: `wait "$CURRENT_CHECK_PID" || row_ok=0` and the orcad leak leg. The row's stdout is never read, and there is no SKIP state. run_gate_mode (7128-7171) only checks exclusions when rc is non-zero, and it reads failures through extract_failed_labels (7066-7068), which matches only `^  <label>: FAIL$`. With no failures it prints "--gate PASS ... every registered check is green at this commit" (7199-7200). I found no environment variable or strict mode that turns a row's SKIP into a non-zero exit. I checked every cited row exit:
- verify-orca-credential-store-live.mjs:120 prints SKIP and returns 0 when typescript is missing. Lines 116-117 do the same with no built PowerBrowser or no orcad.js.
- verify-no-remote-agent-port-live.mjs:286 prints SKIP and returns 0.
- verify-orca-pairing-containment.mjs:257 prints SKIP and returns 0 on pre.skip.
- verify-orca-agent-status-live.mjs:196-200 returns {skip} on a missing build, a missing claude, or an unseeded sign-in. At 395, code stays 0.
- verify-orca-slotless-start.mjs:179 returns 0 on skipReason. scripts/lib/orca-run.mjs:125-133 includes the installed-Orca case, using installedOrcaPaths with home = homedir() (orca-run.mjs:276). Neither path exists on this host now.

The contrast the finding draws is real. rebase-orca.sh:25-28 treats any SKIP line as red in the replay. findings.description: prerequisites() was written for a period when lanes p66-01..p66-03 were unmerged. findings.title: CI never fetches orca/, so the Orca-derived clauses of the quick security rows print SKIP and pass on every push and fork PR

'orca/ is not fetched (bash scripts/fetch-orca.sh)'`)`; verify-orca-failure-classes.mjs:182 (same); verify-orca-browser-entry-points.mjs:659 `if (r.skips.length) { console.log(`${NAME}: SKIP -- ...`); return 0; }`; verify-orca-mobile-protocol.mjs:186 `if (r.skip) return { code: 0, ...
